Two real crises still haven’t woken Europe up https://euobserver.com/245049/one-supply-scare-pushed-china-into-renewables-two-real-crises-still-havent-woken-europe-up/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245049 The mere threat of losing control of one maritime strait turned China into a clean tech powerhouse, while Europe, hit by two real energy shocks in a few years, is wasting time watering down its green rules.]]> In 2003, Chinese president Hu Jintao worried about what became known among the country’s leadership as the ‘Malacca dilemma.’  

Some 80 percent of China’s imported crude passed through the Malacca strait which Beijing’s naval forces could not control. 

This gave rise to a wider security doctrine of supply-chain resilience which became the basis for China’s transformation into the clean tech powerhouse it is today. 

When the US–Iran war disrupted Middle Eastern oil flows this year, Xi Jinping called China’s early bet on wind and solar “forward-looking” – as recounted in a new paper from the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute published on Monday (26 October). 

The paper identifies green growth as “the answer” to geopolitical uncertainty. Clean tech isn’t just clean, it’s also secure and not dependent on imports. Plus, it delivers a “more durable pathway” to “economic resilience.” 

Some governments want to expand fossil-fuel imports, or drill more oil or gas wells, arguing that a more diversified supply chain improves resilience. But the paper dismissed that. 

Oil and gas are priced on global markets, so even producers are exposed to price shocks. More North Sea drilling would save UK households between £16 and £82 (€19 to €98) a year, the paper finds, citing Oxford University research, compared with £105 to £441 on a renewables and electrification pathway.

It’s interesting comparing how the two political systems respond to (hypothetical) supply shocks. In China, the mere threat of losing control of one strait was enough to transform energy politics gradually over many years.

]]> One-in-three European voters now support an authoritarian or populist party, new research reveals https://euobserver.com/245034/one-in-three-european-voters-now-support-an-authoritarian-or-populist-party-new-research-reveals/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 16:21:22 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245034 A historically-high number of voters have chosen parties classified as authoritarian or populist, according to a new report analysing parliamentary election results for 260 parties in 31 countries since 1946, or since the year free elections were first held.]]> A historically-high number of voters have chosen parties classified as authoritarian or populist, according to new research looking at 31 countries across Europe, not just the EU.

Germany saw the starkest rise, with the Alternative for Germany (AfD) getting over 20 percent of the last national parliamentary vote, while in contrast parties classified as radical left split the 13.8 percent of votes between them.

The Authoritarian Populism Index, published by two European think tanks, EPICenter and the Nordics-based Timbro late last week (22 October), analyses parliamentary election results for 260 parties in 31 countries since 1946, or since the year free elections were first held.

The high support for populists is a result of mainstream parties not being able to “adequately address the concerns of our time,” Emelie Franzén, EPICenter’s research coordinator, told EUobserver.

The populists’ success is a “result of a lack of trust towards the elites,” Mateusz Michnik, economic analyst for EPICenter, told EUobserver. He also added that populists are more effective communicators than mainstream parties, especially in crisis situations, such as the Covid pandemic, the migration wave of 2015, or Russia’s 2022 attack on Ukraine.

Read more

Listen: How close is the AfD to governing in Saxony-Anhalt?

The Index has been classifying populist parties since 2016, defining them as groups where representing the people above the elite is “a central organising principle of their political worldview,” the author says.

Despite this overarching characteristic, their profile is far from uniform, the report’s author, Andreas Johansson Heinö, Timbro’s director, warned.

“Most are culturally conservative, while economically they are almost evenly divided between left and right.” The populist parties included in the study tend to be eurosceptic, but only a minority supports leaving the EU, he added.

Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, about 10 percent of Europeans chose authoritarian or populist leaders. Since 2000, the number started to increase, reaching just under 30 percent in 2019.

Now, parties outside of the political mainstream have seats in 11 out of 31 European governments.

“Populists can ‘infect’ other political parties with populism,” Michnik said, which he thinks explains a surge of anti-migration policies across the continent.

Contrary to Germany, Bulgaria, and Norway, which recorded the largest increases in the past years, Hungary’s score radically decreased with the April elections that brought an end to Viktor Orbán’s rule.

]]> Brazil’s Lula survives Bolsonaro scare, safeguarding EU democratic ally on climate and trade https://euobserver.com/245027/brazils-lula-survives-bolsonaro-scare-safeguarding-eu-democratic-ally-on-climate-and-trade/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 16:11:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245027 Brazil's workers' party leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defied all odds to become the first president to win the second round of elections after losing in primaries. Though his adversary has failed to acknowledge defeat, EU leaders and pro-democracy groups expressed relief at the unexpected comeback.]]> In a historic turn of electoral tides, Brazil’s incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated far-right opponent Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday (25 October,) alleviating fears that a Bolsonaro-dynasty comeback would topple the world’s fourth-largest democracy. 

Following a disastrous first-round election for Lula on 4 October, in which he narrowly lost a majority in Brazil’s national congress, the Workers’ party leader overturned predictions to become the first president to win the second round of voting after losing the first one.

First-round voting gave 47 percent for former president Jair Bolsonaro’s son, Flávio, and his rightwing Liberal Party, whose voters mainly represent wealthy and emerging middle classes in the south of Brazil, as well as evangelical Christians, one of the largest religious groups in the country. 

Lula’s northeastern, working class, multi-racial support base only made up 45 percent of all primary votes, but climted to 51.8 percent in Sunday’s second-round of the presidential election. 

Despite setting a record in being the first Brazilian president to win four non-consecutive terms, Lula’s triumph still leaves room for possible conflict. 

Bolsonaro, whose campaign capitalised on continuing the work of his divisive father, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, refused to concede defeat – leaving an open window for history to repeat itself. 

Read more

Trump cheers Bolsonaro Jr’s advance on Lula in Brazil, but EU fears for Mercosur alliance

“We’ll request the annulment of these elections,” Bolsonaro told the press after votes had been counted, accusing Brazil’s Supreme Court of having “changed the rules of the game in the middle of the game,” by ordering polls to stay open for two more hours on Sunday.

What Brazil’s nationalist candidate declared as “unacceptable” was an idea initially intended to facilitate all Brazilians’ attendance at the polls, since multiple areas were reported to have been affected by public transport problems. 

Bolsonaro’s issue with the courts is another link in the chain of power-hungry promises he had made during his campaign to “re-democratise this country”.

Without guidance on what that could mean beyond his publicised desire to extend the duration of presidential terms, many voters fearfully associated his remarks with a potential coup, or with Jair Bolsonaro’s infamous liking for authoritarian rulers – including Brazil’s own 1964-1985 dictatorship.

]]> Ex-EU commissioner Reynders faces new Belgian and Polish scrutiny after EUobserver revelations https://euobserver.com/244962/ex-eu-commissioner-reynders-faces-new-belgian-and-polish-scrutiny-after-euobserver-revelations/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:59:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244962 EUobserver revealed last week that a director in the Belgian intelligence service (VSSE) had exchanged WhatsApp messages with ex-EU commissioner Didier Reynders, which may have been part of a criminal conspiracy to block reports into Reynders' alleged wrongdoing.]]> Some Belgian spies have questioned EUobserver’s report of a cover-up in favour of an allegedly corrupt Belgian ex-EU commissioner, while international commentary focused on his possible Russia ties.

EUobserver revealed on Friday (23 October) that Hugues Brulin, a director in the Belgian intelligence service (VSSE), had exchanged WhatsApp messages with ex-EU commissioner Didier Reynders, which may have been part of a criminal conspiracy to block VSSE reports into Reynders alleged wrongdoing.

But according to “several” VSSE sources who spoke to Belgian daily Le Soir, Brulin, who had been the number three in the hierarchy, had been in charge of logistics, Human Resources, and IT, but did “not have the power to block enquiries or put his nose into dossiers”.

Brulin did have access to secret dossiers only in case the number one and two directors in the VSSE were absent, and he had to sign off on special operations, called “BIMs” in VSSE jargon, which included measures such as phone wiretaps or home intrusions to place bugs, but this situation occurred just once during his tenure, Le Soir said.

But even if that was all true, Brulin still had the power to end the careers of VSSE officers who had looked into Reynders on grounds of flimsy infractions, as happened in at least three cases, according to EUobserver’s sources.

Read more

[EXCLUSIVE] Leaked WhatsApps between ex-EU commissioner Reynders and senior Belgian spy reveal attempts to bury allegations of his possible Russia ties

“This article feels like a liberation. I don’t know if it really is one, but it feels like one … Thanks again in the name of all the normal, honest, taxpaying Belgians,” one ex-VSSE contact told EUobserver, commenting on the article’s revelations.

And besides which, there are allegations that Reynders had other VSSE insiders who might have been better placed to act.

It has received less attention in recent months because there have been more active areas of the front.]]>
  • Ukrainian pressure towards Velyka Novosilka has slowed, but not stopped.
  • The Russian offensive near Orikhiv has stalled, as elsewhere, and Z-channels are again looking for reasons why reality does not match their maps.
  • The weekend was marked by Storm Shadow missiles, which destroyed factories producing Iskander components.
  • Russians are attacking bridges in Zaporizhzhia.
  • Two people died on a train in Voronezh after a Ukrainian drone fell on it; according to the Russians, it was debris from a downed aircraft.
  • Russians destroyed a Czech Dita howitzer.
  • Maps of the day – Velyka Novosilka direction; Orikhiv
  • Videos of the day – destruction of the Czech Dita howitzer; Storm Shadow missiles; a tank destroyed a position on the frontline with direct fire; a MiG-29 shot down a drone.

    • Ukrainian pressure towards Velyka Novosilka has slowed, but not stopped. The battle for Dobropillia continues, but without any major developments. Today, therefore, attention turns to the section of the front that was the main focus in spring, when the Ukrainian army managed to clear hundreds of square kilometres and push the Russians out of 26 villages.

    This is where the borders of three regions meet: Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. It has received less attention in recent months because there have been more active areas of the front, but the creeping Ukrainian counteroffensive has not stopped and the Russians must now seriously consider the risk it poses to their forces in the direction of Velyka Novosilka.

    This town was one of the launching points for the unsuccessful Ukrainian offensive in summer 2023. The Russians captured it in early 2025 and have since moved slowly westwards and north-westwards. They have not got far at all. Following the events of spring, the front is now less than 15 km from Velyka Novosilka.

    Now, under ideal circumstances, the Russian army risks losing some of the gains it has made in this sector during nearly two years of heavy fighting.

    ]]>         Serbia’s student protestors win parliamentary majority – setting scene for showdown with Vučić in December’s presidential poll https://euobserver.com/244879/serbias-student-protestors-win-parliamentary-majority-setting-scene-for-showdown-with-vucic-for-decembers-presidential-poll/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:25:25 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244879 Serbia’s student movement has broken Aleksandar Vučić’s decade-long hold on parliament.]]> “Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future,” said Radomir Sajčić, professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters on Sunday’s evening (25 October). “The voice of the people is being heard”.

    The student-backed list won Serbia’s parliamentary election at the weekend, in a vote that amounts to the biggest challenge so far to president Aleksandar Vučić’s long-standing grip on power.

    And that night, Vučić (unexpectedly) acknowledged defeat. “Vox populi, vox dei,” [The voice of the people is the voice of God], he said, marking a significant moment in the Serbian political landscape that Vučić has dominated for more than a decade.

    The 56-year-old politician served as prime minister from 2014 to 2017, then won the 2017 and 2022 presidential elections. Critics accuse him of authoritarianism, control over the media, and manoeuvring between the European Union, Russia, and China.

    However, this years historic turnout (nearly 70 percent ), the highest since the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1992, has overturned his SNS party (Serbian Progressive Party).

    In the 250-seat parliament, the Student’s List will have the majority – 140 seats, and second comes Vučić’s SNS with 104 seats. The remaining seats will be shared mainly between ethnic national-⁠minority parties.  

    “It was effectively a referendum on president Aleksandar Vučić,” the Serbian pro-democracy group Kreni-Promeni, who backed the Students’ List, told EUobserver.

    From student protests to electoral change

    The opposition was unable to seriously challenge Vučić in the previous parliamentary elections, partly because of its fragmentation. However, a significant turning point in Serbian politics came in November 2024, when 16 people died after a canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad.

    Read more

    Serbian students and diaspora maintain pressure for Vučić to call elections, with no EU help

    The tragedy then sparked massive demonstrations across Serbia, led primarily by students. Hundreds of thousands of people took part. They blamed the disaster largely on the government and its corruption.

    The student protests gave rise to Vučić’s main challenger in this year’s elections: the Student List (SL). The 250 candidates running for parliament included individuals selected by students, primarily academics.

    “The students have selected prominent citizens – experts in their own fields,” Miloje Savić, a volunteering poll observer, told EUobserver. “They know which values they are supposed to protect and represent,” he added.

    The student electoral list was led by Ilija Srdanović, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in Novi Sad.

    The weekend result thus represent a major political breakthrough for a movement that emerged less than two years ago from protests against the government’s long-standing corruption.

    For the SNS, this defeat is “a huge blow to him [Vučić]”, senior research associate at the University of Belgrade, Jelena Vasiljević told EUobserver.

    But, as the poll winner and Vučić’s most successful opponent, the SL is not out of the woods yet.

    Students smeared as ‘blockaders‘

    Even as he acknowledged defeat, Vučić continued to use the same online rhetoric, referring to winners as the “students’ blockade list”. Vučić also warned of investor uncertainty and damage these results might have on the gas trade.

    Taken together – the language and the economic warnings – offer an insight into how the SNS and Vučić will depict the incoming government.

    “They would be framing the student movement as not as a legitimate political power, but as an extension of the protest movement and as a risk to economic stability,” Vanesa Valcheva, head of research at Balkan Free Media Initiative (BFMI), told EUobserver.

    ]]>         Czech government approves first step to scrapping TV and radio licence fees in 4.36am vote, sparking protests https://euobserver.com/244873/czech-government-approves-first-step-to-scrapping-tv-and-radio-licence-fees-in-4-36am-vote-sparking-protests/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 11:29:49 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244873 If changes pass, citizens will no longer pay licence fees toward Czech Television and Czech Radio, and the government will instead fund public media operations from the state budget. Opposition MPs and experts have described these far-reaching changes as a dangerous attempt to weaken public service media, threatening their independence.]]> First published in Deník N.

    The lower house of Czech parliament became a nighttime battleground for the future of the country’s public service media at the weekend, when MPs pushed through the abolition of public service media licence fees in the bill’s first reading in the chamber on Saturday (24 October).

    Czech MPs voted to pass a bill that lays the groundwork to abolish TV and radio licence fees and move public media under the state budget.

    The weekend vote was not yet a vote on the law’s final approval: the government coalition only needed to prevent the bill’s rejection which the opposition had sought.

    The controversial vote was scheduled for 4.36am on Saturday – by no means a typical time for such a vote. Opposition parties had failed to postpone the vote, and also did not have enough numbers to reject the bill.

    Out of 177 lawmakers present, 96 MPs voted in favour of the bill, while 81 opposition MPs voted to reject it. Prime minister Andrej Babiš did not take part in the vote.

    MPs from the Czech Republic’s five opposition parties also failed to pass a proposal to return the bill for redrafting to the coalition formed by ANO (led by the PM) and the far-right parties Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) and Motorists to Themselves.

    The bill will now go to the parliament’s media and culture committee. This will be followed by lengthy debate at the law’s second reading, where amendments may be submitted. The proceedings will likely last several days.

    Read more

    PM Babiš blames press for ANO election loss, renews calls to abolish license fees for Czech public media

    4.36am vote planned at last-minute

    Babiš’s governing majority only added the agenda item for ending licence fees on the Chamber of Deputies’ (lower house of parliament’s) agenda on Friday morning. It even took by surprise the MPs of ANO, SPD and Motorists.

    The coalition leadership formed by Babiš and foreign minister Petr Macinka (Motorists) had kept the plan secret all week, so that it would not become public and opposition parties could not prepare obstruction tactics.

    Protesters had gathered outside the parliament through the night in the early hours of Saturday morning. Demonstrations carried on throughout the Czech Republic over the weekend.

Netanyahu may fall on Tuesday, but the West Bank annexation policies won’t https://euobserver.com/244874/i-led-israels-oldest-peace-group-and-advised-the-knesset-netanyahu-may-fall-on-tuesday-but-the-west-bank-annexation-policies-wont/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 11:21:29 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244874 Israel's election on Tuesday could bring a new government without changing the country's course. Having worked as a parliamentary adviser in the Knesset and later as executive director of Peace Now, I know how that can happen, writes Shaqued Morag.]]> Israel’s election on Tuesday (27 October) could bring a new government without changing the country’s course. Having worked as a parliamentary adviser in the Knesset and later as executive director of Peace Now, I know how that can happen.

    Many of the parties seeking to replace Benjamin Netanyahu are avoiding clear positions on the Israeli-Palestinian question, but some of their candidates may end up overseeing annexation they never campaigned for.

    Israel’s previous coalition, led by Naftali Bennett in 2021, offers a warning.

    Called the “government of change” because it ended Netanyahu’s 12-year run in office, it brought together a variety of parties, from Bennett’s rightwing party to Labor and Meretz, leftwing parties.

    Its answer to profound ideological disagreements, particularly over the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, was to preserve the status quo. The coalition lasted roughly 18 months, and although it changed the tone of government, it left much of the policy towards the West Bank intact.

    Read more

    No candidate in Israeli election backs a Palestinian state. The EU’s answer is more ‘reforms’, not pressure

    For example, Merav Michaeli, then Labor leader and transport minister, opposed settlement expansion.

    Yet her ministry continued to implement previously approved infrastructure commitments, including substantial budgets for roads facilitating that expansion.

    Through my work at Peace Now, I saw how the coalition’s status-quo agreement constrained her ability to challenge projects inherited from the previous government. A minister could thus find herself implementing a vision she opposed.

    Today, the stakes are higher.

    Another slice of the West Bank

    Consider E1, between Jerusalem and the settlement of Ma’ale Adumim, where construction would threaten Palestinian territorial contiguity and the viability of a future Palestinian state.

    The government has advanced tenders for all 3,401 planned housing units, with crucial stages of the tender process set to be completed before a new government takes office.

    E1 exemplifies wider efforts to establish difficult-to-reverse facts: new settlement outposts, including in areas under Palestinian civil administration, expanding settlements and administrative changes that entrench Israeli control.

    A successor government would have to intervene actively to reverse them.

    These developments are backed by an explicit political vision. The current government’s guidelines and coalition agreements assert exclusive Jewish rights throughout the land of Israel and commit to advancing Israeli sovereignty in the West Bank.

    Under Bezalel Smotrich, serving as a minister within the defence ministry, a new settlement administration and civilian positions have been established, shifting significant aspects of West Bank governance from military administration to civilian political control.

    These structures will not disappear when their architects leave office. The far-right has equipped the state with both a vision and the machinery to advance it.

    Inertia is not neutral when the machinery is already moving in one direction.

    Parties seeking to replace Netanyahu need not necessarily agree on a final-status agreement with the Palestinians, but they must find enough common ground to commit to halting annexation and reversing the structures that enable it.

    Those understandings belong in coalition negotiations, when parties still have leverage, rather than in battles left for individual ministers once they are in office.

    Nor is this a distant constitutional question.     “The two-state solution is not really on the menu in the Jewish Israeli political mainstream”

    The liberal Zionists are united around their secularism and their commitment to the liberal democratic institutions, but there’s one big caveat: when it comes to the Palestinian issue, their liberalism is more circumscribed. 

    They are not talking about the ongoing occupation and the effect that that has on Israel’s democratic standing. But of course, they’re very united in their opposition to Netanyahu.

    The liberal Zionist camp lacks a coherent platform other than this; they basically advocate for good governance, but don’t offer a robust vision. 

    And that cannot be said about the nationalists, whose vision is quite clear, right?

    Traditionally, the nationalist camp was the mainstream right wing. Today’s main contenders are prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu.

    Meanwhile, former prime minister Naftali Bennett is running on a joint list with Lapid’s Yesh Atid, called Beyachad (‘Together’). Bennett and Lapid joined forces despite coming from different ideological traditions. They have very different ideas about the country, but they’re coming together to present a more technocratic agenda, get Netanyahu out and normalise Israeli politics. 

    Read more

    EU risks funding Israeli firms which help develop NAZA-type violent tech

    The nationalist camp descends from the Revisionist Zionist tradition based on Ze’ev Jabotinsky’s vision: a liberal democratic outlook fused with ultra-nationalist convictions. So to take a Revisionist Zionist view is to take a hawkish and hardline approach towards Arabs, while keeping a commitment to liberal democratic values. But affinity for liberalism and democratic values has really withered away over recent decades, not only under Netanyahu.

    And then there is the ultra-Orthodox camp, without which the current government would never have completed a full term.

    The ultra-Orthodox group does not fit easily on the left-to-right political spectrum, which in the Israeli understanding is defined by hawkishness on Palestinians and security.

    They are made up of two Ashkenazi parties – Degel HaTorah and Agudat Yisrael – and Sephardic party Shas. What unites them is strict religious observance of Jewish law and their commitment to separation from secular society or modernity.

    “The ultra-Orthodox camp is predominantly non-Zionist, but not necessarily anti-Zionist”

    Interestingly, the ultra-Orthodox camp is predominantly non-Zionist, but not necessarily anti-Zionist since they didn’t endorse the creation of Israel in its secular form. They engage with the state, but in a limited way – they’re very transactional and pragmatic.

    And the ultra-orthodox camp work within state apparatus to advance sectoral interests, yeshiva education, the military service exemption, and subsidies to maintain a somewhat introverted separation from the rest of society.

    They are mostly passive when it comes to issues of foreign policy and security policy, but they do not support loss of Jewish life for nationalist ends – they don’t believe that the state in its current form is sacred. And so they don’t, for instance, endorse the loss of Jewish life for territorial expansion.

    Read more

    No Israeli bonds on sale in EU for now, in de facto €2.2bn sanction

    That leaves us with the last category: the religious nationalist camp.

    Religious nationalists draw together ultra-orthodox religious observance, but with ultra-nationalism.

    ]]>         Moscow elites pleased with US envoy Witkoff and far from agreeing to peace (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,702) https://euobserver.com/244704/moscow-elites-pleased-with-us-envoy-witkoff-and-far-from-agreeing-to-peace-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1702/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:07:29 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244704 Starshield, the defense version of Starlink, seems to remain slow despite US assurances that it was fully back. And journalists from Russia reveal what is being discussed by Kremlin and US officials as they seek a deal on Ukraine.]]>
  • Russian journalists reveal what the Kremlin and US are discussing.
  • Starshield was supposedly fixed, but that doesn’t seem to be the case.
  • Russians advance in Rai-Oleksandrivka towards Sloviansk.
  • Russia loses two combat Sukhoi aircraft in accidents in one day.
  • Map of the day: Rai-Oleksandrivka
  • Videos of the day: Kramatorsk evacuation; Russian Su-30 crashes; how helicopters hunt drones.

    • Russian journalists have described the nature of talks between the Kremlin and the US. A demilitarised zone in Donbas. A Ukraine without Nato membership but is allowed to join the EU membership in return. Sanctions against Russia eased, Russian gas in Europe and news talks on the Nord Stream 2 pipeline. And America makes its own deals with Russia.

    This is how, according to The Economist, the US proposal to the Kremlin for ending the war sounded, presented in Moscow on Wednesday (21 October) by Steve Witkoff, Trump’s negotiator.

    It sounds like something Russia might welcome, but that does not appear to be the case. At least not according to the findings of the Russian exile website Verstka, which a day later published an extensive report on the mood among Russia’s Kremlin-linked elite.

    The article, signed by the newspaper’s editorial board, contains numerous quotes from government officials and people close to the regime, whose views on the prospect of swiftly reaching a peace deal and ending the fighting are sceptical.

    Verstka wrote that war fatigue was mounting among these people, whose names it naturally did not disclose, but that they fully defer to Russian president Vladimir Putin and are waiting to see what he agrees with US president Donald Trump.

    “It can be said with certainty that American sympathies have shifted to our side. We have been working on this for a year and a half,” a source close to the foreign ministry told the journalists, describing Moscow’s strategy.

    Russia achieved this through the following argument: since Ukraine considers itself a victim — which it undoubtedly is, editor’s note — and asks for assistance, but is unwilling to make concessions in return for that assistance, it is no longer in fact a victim, but a player with ambitions of its own, which Western taxpayers are unwilling to fund.

    Incidentally, the Slovak government uses very similar rhetoric and arguments.

    According to the same source, Moscow will emphasise during the talks the hopelessness of Ukraine’s supposed situation.

    Another quoted voice was a political strategist directly linked to the Kremlin, who pointed out that Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner did not directly take part in the talks in St Petersburg on 21 October, reportedly due to illness.

    Nevertheless, this source also praised the US approach, even if Trump’s dispute with Ukraine proved only short-lived: “We have nothing to lose from these solutions. And we could gain both an improved budget and an advantage on the battlefield.” At the same time, the domestic political strategist saw no fundamental changes that could lead to an end to the fighting.

    The extent of the irrationality prevailing within the regime was illustrated by statements from another unnamed representative of a formally non-governmental organisation working directly with the Kremlin.

    In his analysis, he claimed that Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky had created a dictatorial system from which neither elections nor a coup could remove him, and that the war would not end while he remained in office. He also cited reports by Russia’s foreign intelligence service claiming that Kyiv was cooperating with Mexican drug cartels.

    Another government official had low expectations of the Americans: “For almost two years now, we have been saying that Trump is supposedly one of us and that the talks are constructive, but they have produced no results. We are fighting, burning, drowning, suffering alongside our homeland.”

    The man spoke of a “peace wing”, allegedly comprising people in the presidential administration responsible for domestic policy and economic circles, but this did not mean that there was any open opposition to the war.

    “There is no escape from the ship. We are waiting for them to have had enough of the war,” the official said.

    ]]>         New EU-wide asylum law ends up in court in Italy https://euobserver.com/244651/new-eu-wide-asylum-law-ends-up-in-court-in-italy/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 14:22:27 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244651 An Egyptian national who sought protection in Italy after arriving on the island of Lampedusa in August may end up dealing a constitutional blow to the EU's asylum laws after seeking legal counsel. ]]> An Egyptian national who sought protection in Italy after arriving on the island of Lampedusa in August may end up dealing a constitutional blow to the EU’s asylum laws after seeking legal counsel.

    The Egyptian, who is not named, had his asylum claim rejected even though he did not understand his translator. His is appealing.

    “Not even European Union law can conflict with our supreme principles,” his lawyer, Claudia Avenia told EUobserver earlier this week.

    Aside from his own personal circumstances, his legal case is raising serious issues that could have a knock-on effect on the EU’s new asylum and migration pact, which kicked into force this past June across all 27 EU member states.

    Because he is from Egypt, he was shuffled through a fast track asylum procedure. EU laws require the accelerated process from nationals who have a 20 percent chance or less of getting asylum in Europe. Egypt fits into this category.

    A new EU law also meant that he was technically not yet legally inside the EU as authorities carried out health checks, identification and other assessments during a so-called pre-screening phase.

    It means he was banned from stepping outside a reception centre, where he was being housed.

    Lawyers describe it as the legal fiction of non-entry, similar in scope to certain areas of international airports. Rights experts had earlier warned, when the EU rules were being drafted, that this would lead to defacto detention.

    Read more

    French push for legal limbos on EU borders

    ]]>         Jewish groups clash over whether EU antisemitism envoy should influence Israel policy, as controversial von Schnurbein goes back to Berlin https://euobserver.com/244650/jewish-groups-clash-over-whether-eu-antisemitism-envoy-should-influence-israel-policy-as-controversial-von-schnurbein-goes-back-to-berlin/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 13:49:37 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244650 Katharina von Schnurbein caused controversy in May 2025 when she briefed EU ambassadors in Tel Aviv that proposed EU trade sanctions on Israel were based on "rumours about Jews, as opposed to facts".]]> Two leading Jewish groups want the EU’s next antisemitism tsar to also brief diplomats on foreign policy – despite the controversy it caused for the last one, Katharina von Schnurbein.

    “EU external decisions have direct consequences for Jews living in Europe. Diplomats should hear from the person who sees those consequences every day,” said Pinchas Goldschmidt, who heads the Conference of European Rabbis (CER) in Munich, Germany.

    The European Jewish Congress (EJC) in Brussels also told EUobserver: “The [EU antisemitism] coordinator should ensure that this objective is systematically reflected in all relevant EU policies, including external action and foreign policy.”

    They spoke as von Schnurbein prepared to leave her EU post after 10 years to become a German “federal government commissioner for Jewish life in Germany and the fight against antisemitism” on 28 October.

    The 53-year-old German baroness was highly active at events in EU capitals, had three staff, and travelled on missions to Israel, Serbia, Switzerland, and the US.

    She also worked next door to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen in her Brussels HQ and had close ties with the Israeli government.

      <title>Anthropic files for potentially record-breaking stock market valuation in key test for AI industry</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/anthropic-files-listing-stock-market</link>
      <description><p>Market debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viability</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/anthropic">Anthropic</a> has publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US market will serve as a test of the financial viability of the multitrillion-dollar AI boom.</p><p>Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/jun/01/anthropic-ai-ipo">confidentially filed</a> with US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/anthropic-files-listing-stock-market">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Meta says share sale will support its “continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”, as<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/26/ai-cloud-computing-companies-guppy-level-death-elon-musk-stock-markets-dollar-oil-bond-yieds-latest-news-updates?page=with%3Ablock-6adef8968f08a448dcaddf6f#block-6adef8968f08a448dcaddf6f"> Elon Musk warns some AI cloud computing firms face ‘guppy-level death’</a></p><p><strong>UK government borrowing costs are dropping this morning, a welcome sign ahead of Wednesday’s budget.</strong></p><p>The yield (or interest rate) on 10 and 30-year UK gilts have both dropped by around three basis points (0.03 of a percentage point) this morning.</p><p>Issuing loans to public financial institutions creates a financial asset that offsets the increase in outstanding government debt.       <title>The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/y2k-used-cars-gen-z</link>
      <description><p>People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans</p><p>Jack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.</p><p>Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/y2k-used-cars-gen-z">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comTue, 27 Oct 2026 04:48:05 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[AI boom and simmering oil prices boost global stocks, but Brazil election knocks some back]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/ai-boom-and-simmering-oil-prices-boost-global-stocks-but-brazil-election-knocks-some-back/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/ai-boom-and-simmering-oil-prices-boost-global-stocks-but-brazil-election-knocks-some-back/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:10:11 +0000Global stocks grew steadily Monday, as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom on Wall Street bolstered the New York stock market and simmering oil prices gave US investors renewed confidence in the energy industry.

Elsewhere, responses to the re-election of the left-wing presidential incumbent in Brazil knocked many Spanish and Portuguese companies back, as traders hedge their bets on the economic future of the growing superpower.

Dublin

The Iseq All-Share index ended the opening day of trading in the green, growing 1.54 per cent to 14,153.02 by close of markets Monday, with only two listed companies falling in share value.

Housebuilders Glenveagh Properties dipped 0.21 per cent at €2.42 a share, while insurance company FBD Holdings fell 0.78 per cent to close at €19.10. Mining company Kenmare Resources and ferry-operator Irish Continental Group saw no change in their share prices.

Ryanair’s stock took off, up 2.04 per cent to close at €22.99, while the banking sector saw steady growth as well: Bank of Ireland rising 1.79 per cent at €18.24 and AIB following suit, growing 1.34 per cent to €10.96 a share.

Nutrition firm Origins increased 6.44 per cent in stock price, ending the day at €4.30 a share, and building materials specialist Kingspan seeing steady growth of 3.02 per cent to €92.05 by close.

London

The London Stock Exchange began the trading week on a positive note, in part thanks to strong returns from the city’s financial services sector. The blue-chip FTSE 100 rose 0.69 per cent by close, while the mid-cap FTSE 250 index jumped 1.06 per cent.

Lloyds bank saw its share price increase 1.84 per cent, following on a similarly steading trading week last week, while its industry rival Barclays did one better, up 2.89 per cent by close, as investors noted the Bank of England signalled higher interest rates could soon come into play.

British oil and gas giant BP dropped 1.21 per cent, while C&C – the drinks groups with Asahi and Bulmers in its portfolio – also fell, closing the day 1.54 per cent down.

Europe

Elsewhere in Europe, stocks across the Continent saw steady growth as the trading week began, although the results of the Brazilian presidential election ricocheted across national economies on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean.

Shares in Santander bank slid 3.24 per cent downwards by close of markets as the Spanish financial institution, whose primary subsidiary outside of Europe is located in Brazil, reckoned with the re-election of left-wing Lula da Silva over far-right Jair Bolsonaro.

Meanwhile, Portuguese energy provider Galp Energia suffered larger losses, with its share price plummeting 10.84 per cent, in some part due to the uncertainty of its linguistic neighbour, but also the collapse of merger talks with Madrid-based energy company Moeve.

France’s luxury industry somewhat recuperated last week’s declines, as Hermès grew its share price 3.31 per cent by close, following a poor week of trading due to lower-than-expected financial results being published.

New York

Early trades on Wall Street were bolstered by renewed confidence from investors in AI stock and brief respite from soaring oil prices.

Before midday New York time, the Nasdaq 100 index jumped some 1.25 per cent, while the S&P 500 hovered about 0.75 per cent up from Friday’s close of market price point and the Dow Jones Industrial Average trailed behind, rising 0.20 per cent or so.

As US officials and representatives from their allies in the Middle East traveled to Iran in a bid to defuse rising tensions, the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil (the industry benchmark) fell below $115, having soared last week to levels not seen since May.

Anthropic, the AI programmers behind the Claude chatbot, released its prospectus earlier in the day, detailing the exponential growth that has led it to a $965 billion valuation in its latest private funding round in May. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg.

]]>Michael Nagle<![CDATA[Pilot fatigue risk badly managed in Ireland, says international survey]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/26/pilot-fatigue-risk-badly-managed-in-ireland-says-international-survey/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/26/pilot-fatigue-risk-badly-managed-in-ireland-says-international-survey/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:59:05 +0000Irish pilots say that fatigue is badly managed by the air travel industry here while some fear reporting the problem to their employer, according to an international survey.

The news prompted trade unionists to demand greater Government and regulatory oversight of the risk after the survey showed the Republic lags much of Europe in managing the problem.

European rules limit the hours that pilots can fly to 13 a-day and 60 in one week, and allow them to report unfit for flying if they feel fatigued.

But most Irish pilots say the issue is poorly managed here while some say they do not report as unfit due to fatigue as they fear “punishment”, according to a survey by trade union group, the European Cockpit Association.

Around half of European pilots say they flew fatigued recently while three out of four have experienced “micro sleeps” while on duty, states the survey of 7,200 pilots from 32 countries.

The Irish Airline Pilots’ Association (Ialpa) called for greater oversight of the issue in the Republic.

Capt Nicola Hughes, the trade union’s international director, said Minister for Transport, Darragh O’Brien, should appoint inspectors to ensure that airlines comply with employment law and allow pilots to exercise their safety responsibilities without fear of consequences.

The report, which does not name any Irish airline, shows that 71.5 per cent of pilots in the Republic say fatigue risk is “not well managed” or “mostly not well managed”, against slightly more than half for Europe as a whole.

In the last such survey in 2023, 61.7 per cent of Irish pilots criticised their employers’ fatigue management.

The ECA report notes that the Republic and Malta performed poorly relative to the rest of Europe this year and in 2023.

“Ireland is at or near the bottom across a range of critical fatigue-management and reporting measures, and in several areas the position has deteriorated rather than improved,” said Hughes.

Almost four in 10 pilots in Europe say that fear of punishment deters them from reporting that they are unfit to fly due to fatigue.

Of Irish pilots, only 3.6 per cent say they trust the reporting system, the lowest in Europe. The average is 12 per cent.

Hughes said that the responses required clear responses from the air travel safety regulator, Irish Aviation Authority and Government.

She called for strengthened independent oversight of fatigue management and employment practices.

Welcoming the survey the authority said it reinforced the importance of “effective, proactive management of fatigue risks” by airlines.

“European flight time limitation rules establish a common safety baseline, and operators are responsible for identifying and managing fatigue risks through their management systems, taking account of their specific operations,” the regulator pointed out.

The IAA added that its oversight of Irish airlines included consistently assessing and evaluating their application of flight-time rules.

Aer Lingus, one of the country’s two biggest airlines did not comment.

The airline has established protocols for reporting fatigue, according to a source familiar with the industry.

Ryanair had not responded to a request for comment by the time of going to press.

]]>Michal Krakowiak<![CDATA[Beacon Hospital delivers €5.7m profit in first full year under Macquarie ownership]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/beacon-hospital-delivers-57m-profit-in-first-full-year-under-macquarie-ownership/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/beacon-hospital-delivers-57m-profit-in-first-full-year-under-macquarie-ownership/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 16:15:18 +0000The Beacon Hospital group at Sandyford in south Dublin last year returned to an operating profit as revenues surged by 49 per cent.

New consolidated accounts filed by Macquarie asset management firm, MEIF 7 DIAN Investments Limited, show the hospital delivered an operating profit of €5.69 million after an operating loss of €2.39 million in 2024.

Revenues jumped to €288.58 million from €193.66 million the previous year though that comparison is skewed as Macquarie did not complete the acquisition until the first half of 2024 after the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) cleared the purchase in February 2024.

The world’s largest infrastructure manager paid €324 million for the hospital group, which had primarily been owned up to that by businessman Denis O’Brien.

The hospital group – which also operates outreach clinics in Limerick and Mullingar – recorded a pretax loss of €11.1 million last year. This, it said, was due to interest costs and similar charges of €16.8 million – mainly to a connected party.

The pretax loss also takes account of combined non-cash depreciation and amortisation costs of €35.25 million.

The group sustained a loss after tax of €14.56 million after paying €3.44 million in corporation tax.

The directors noted that the reported loss reflected accounting adjustments, primarily the goodwill amortisation of €21.4 million and related-party interest costs of €15.7 million, rather than underlying operational performance of the business.

The hospital “continues to deliver year-on-year growth in patient demand, supported by strong and collaborative partnerships with private insurers under robust reimbursement models”, they said.

A €100 million redevelopment of the adjacent former Beacon Hotel site is currently under way to create an eight-storey medical facility adjoining the current hospital.

Scheduled to open next summer, the directors said the expansion would increase patient capacity by approximately 40 per cent, adding 70 new inpatient beds, a state-of-the-art emergency department, six new surgical theatres and a new cancer day unit. It will create 350 new jobs and facilitate the recruitment of more than 100 specialist consultants.

The hospital, which first opened 20 years ago, said it accommodated more than 295,000 patient visits last year under the care of more than 410 consultants.

Numbers employed last year increased from 1,504 to 1,565 as staff costs increased from €83.3 million to €119.8 million.

]]>Matt Kavanagh<![CDATA[AI firm Anthropic begins countdown to IPO with prospectus filing]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/26/anthropic-begins-countdown-to-ipo-with-prospectus-filing/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/26/anthropic-begins-countdown-to-ipo-with-prospectus-filing/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:54:20 +0000Anthropic has fired the starting gun on one of the largest-ever initial public offerings, unveiling its pitch for a listing that is set to be the biggest test so far of investor appetite for the artificial intelligence boom.

The developer of Claude published its highly anticipated prospectus on Monday, detailing for the first time how it plans to sustain the exponential growth that propelled the company from a $183 billion (€163.5 billion) valuation just over a year ago to $965 billion in its last private funding round in May.

The group recently told backers that its third-quarter revenue had jumped nearly 50 per cent on the previous three months to $16.8 billion and that the company was profitable on an adjusted basis.

The nearly 240,000-word prospectus showed that in the first half of the year, Anthropic’s net loss was $81 billion, with more than $72 billion related to changes in the value of convertible notes as the company’s valuation increased.

The bulk of the remaining losses come from a near-$9 billion outlay on computing power and infrastructure.

The document also said that Anthropic plans to aggressively increase its spending in the years to come, with commitments totalling close to $800 billion over the coming decade.

Goldman Sachs was listed as having secured the coveted “lead left” role in Anthropic’s IPO.

Anthropic’s founders said AI could “raise productivity across every sector of the economy” but also warned its models “have become better able to circumvent” systems designed to make sure they act as intended. It added that it has documented cases where models “manipulate or subvert” monitoring.

The company also pointed to risks stemming from a small number of high-value clients that account for a large slice of its revenues. While it noted that “no single customer” represented more than 10 per cent of its revenue in the nine months to September, Anthropic said that a quarter over the period came from its “top five” clients.

The San Francisco-based group is pressing ahead with the IPO at a critical juncture for the AI industry, as a furious debate rages over the safety of the technology and concerns grow over whether the increasingly debt-fuelled investment boom will pay off.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 has fallen just over 7 per cent from a record high touched on October 6th.

In a sign of the more testing backdrop, existing Anthropic investors expect the company to seek a valuation of between $1.5 trillion and $1.75 trillion. In August, several of Anthropic’s backers had said they expected the group to list at a valuation of $2 trillion or more.

In its prospectus, the company’s founders said the advice they had received from multiple partners was: “Never let your company be worth a dollar more than it is actually worth.”

The publication of the prospectus puts Anthropic on track to list after the US midterm elections on November 3rd, in which the benefits and costs of the AI boom have emerged as a central issue for voters, but before the Thanksgiving holiday on November 26th.

Disclosing the prospectus is likely to ease the nerves of investors who feared that Anthropic’s window to go public was rapidly closing. It is rare for companies to list between the Thanksgiving holiday and the end of the year.

]]>KIRAN RIDLEY<![CDATA[Across-the-board pay rise will do little to help fill key public sector posts]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/26/across-the-board-pay-rise-will-do-little-to-help-fill-key-public-sector-posts/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/26/across-the-board-pay-rise-will-do-little-to-help-fill-key-public-sector-posts/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:38:00 +0000

Until the early 1970s, the Civil Service was a very traditional organisation that had changed little over time. There was limited movement between departments, and almost none between the public sector and the private sector.

Most people joined straight after school, there were few graduates, although many ambitious civil servants, like TK Whitaker, studied for a degree at night. Unless they were women who married [and who were effectively fired as a result], civil servants were likely to stay until they retired. Men progressed slowly through the ranks, based on seniority.

My first boss in the Department of Finance told me that when he joined it in the 1950s, he had calculated, based on the seniority rule and his colleagues’ ages, that he would spend most of his career as an assistant principal before, in the final three years before retirement, being promoted in rapid succession as a principal officer and then assistant secretary. In the event, he served as secretary general of the department for seven years.

Joining the EU meant quite a number of Irish civil servants left to work for the European Commission. The marriage bar ended in July 1973. Gradually, other reforms led to much more fluid movement across the public service.

The wider public service included graduate roles such as secondary teachers, doctors and local-authority engineers. While less than a third of public servants held third-level qualifications in 1970, those who did constituted more than half of the Irish graduate workforce.

All of this made public sector employment rather different from that in the private sector, with limited parallels in terms of pay. To a large extent, public and private sector employers were not competing to attract the same workers.

The advent of mass third level education in Ireland changed things. Few now enter the public sector straight from school. Primary teachers and nurses now have graduate qualifications. Today, three quarters of public sector workers have a third level qualification, but only constitute a third of graduate workers.

There is also greater choice, and substantial movement, between jobs in the public and private sectors. The security of a public sector job does not have the same allure when there is full employment. So the State as an employer needs to compete to attract and retain talent. That means the public sector must pay competitive rates, or some of the most able and ambitious teachers, civil servants, nurses or physiotherapists will seek better pay elsewhere.

Are public sector workers all as badly off as strikes might suggest? This is what the data says

In the run-up to the 2008 economic crash, average pay in the public sector had reached 50 per cent more than in the private sector – an excessive gap.

Following the collapse in the public finances, all public sector workers experienced painful cuts in pay. Over the subsequent decade, public service pay rose more slowly than the private sector. However, over the past few years the relationship has stabilised.

Public service workers are paid, on average, about 30 per cent more than the private sector, but this largely reflects their higher average qualifications.

The Government now needs to deliver a pay increase for public service workers, not because prices are higher but because most other workers are seeing their pay rise. Failure to keep pace with the private sector would see skilled employees leave.

The Department of Finance forecast that average pay across the economy will rise by around 4 per cent this year and next. The budget arithmetic provided for a 3 per cent public pay rise next year, so any higher pay deal will need additional funding.

The expected rise in private sector pay sets a guideline for any public sector pay agreement. If public sector workers are offered significantly more, that could push up taxes, and have knock-on effects on other pay. But if offered significantly less than their private sector counterparts, there could be an exodus of skilled staff for better pay elsewhere.

A public pay deal will be done – and here’s what it will look like

While this sounds fairly straightforward, things are, of course, more complex. Private sector pay deals are generally contingent on increased productivity. That, too, should be the case in the public sector.

Across-the-board pay increases in the public sector won’t address what’s needed to attract workers to some key areas where posts have been hard to fill – in the Naval Service, in special care, in some IT roles.

While a private employer would simply pay more, public pay agreements cannot easily handle such differentiation, but need to find a way to do so. The alternative of filling key roles by outsourcing to consultants is not an ideal one.

]]>Chris Maddaloni<![CDATA[With EU presidency, Ireland has chance to implement digital identity wallet by end of year ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/with-eu-presidency-ireland-has-chance-to-implement-digital-identity-wallet-by-end-of-year/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/with-eu-presidency-ireland-has-chance-to-implement-digital-identity-wallet-by-end-of-year/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:27:00 +0000The priorities for Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the EU have been wide in scope across various sections of society, different sectors within the economy, along with competing national or common interests.

Some of those will resolve in due course under the current term, while many will either stall or progress as it passes onto Lithuania and then Greece through 2027.

One long-standing objective and policy priority that falls directly during our watch is the provision for an EU Digital Identity Wallet for all citizens and businesses by December of this year.

This is part of the wider Digital Decade Policy Programme (DDPP), which is the EU’s framework for achieving digital transformation by the end of the decade.

It includes targets in relation to digital skills, digital infrastructure, the digitalisation of businesses, and access to digital public services.

That last (but not least) area essentially involves all key public services being available online with citizens’ digital identity and ability to access services working seamlessly throughout the EU.

The practical applications are complex but the “only once” principle applies throughout, where citizens should not be repeatedly asked by governments or multiple agencies for information already available.

With progress being made on all fronts to various degrees, this is now a defining period for Ireland to help push the digital public services agenda forward for citizens, businesses and State services. Interoperable data should flow freely enough to support everything from mortgage approvals to healthcare records and planning applications.

The main challenge is one that often falls on European or cross-border projects. It comes down to collective co-ordination and consensus. Twenty-seven member states, with as many starting points, governance structures, all building toward the same targets along separate paths that sometimes fail to intersect.

The issues to be resolved don’t solely lie within policy, legal or technological constraints. It is often social where the connectivity falls down. How do people, who each hold a piece of a public problem, find one another, build trust, and produce outcomes that outlast a ministerial photocall or presidential term? The EU and the Irish Government have invested heavily in the building blocks that are needed for this journey. The digital identity wallets, data spaces and cloud platforms already exist.

What is missing is the right people coming together from different corners, knowing how to assemble these blocks in the right way.

Practitioners who have the ability and mindset to move between a Brussels regulation and a rural county council’s operating reality, without treating the two as separate jobs.

Ireland’s role in this during its EU presidency is reflected in a new initiative that will gather the necessary stakeholders to generate those collective solutions for the next phase of Europe’s digital public services roadmap.

To break the roadblocks and unlock the capabilities that can advance these future services, we need to first go back though to an age-old practice. Before internet technology, quantum computing or artificial intelligence were even imagined, Ireland had meitheal.

This was among our oldest social networks and was based on reciprocity, trust and shared responsibilities. Its approach was replicated in similiar forms in different countries: Norway’s dugnad, Finland’s talkoot, Lithuania’s talka, Hungary’s kaláka and the Balkan moba.

Each European tradition reflects the same civic principle that complex problems can be solved when communities pool effort, skills and responsibility. It activated to do work that no single person or household could manage alone.

The main rule being that help given would be returned. This created a social infrastructure and self-enforcing system for dedicating skills exactly when and where they were needed. That practice and principle may be what is needed now to push forward on Ireland and Europe’s digital public services programme.

On November 19th and 20th, Ireland will hold the first Meitheal Digiteach that will bring policy makers, community groups, data designers, delivery practitioners, architects and engineers into the same room to work through the shared challenges, while looking to create practical solutions and connect the diverging tracks on the new Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) rails.

The gathering will not work like a regular conference with the usual panel discussions, keynote addresses and firesides or roundtables. This will be a hands-on exercise for participants with no hierarchy and no spectators.

It is due to be held at a fitting location within the Drogheda Civic Offices which, since its relatively recent refurbishment, now represents a suitable blend of heritage with modern design and functionality. The call is for like-minded citizens and groups to get involved in building the next level of digital public services.

I’d encourage all who have a role to play to join us, as Ireland’s meitheal provides a mechanism that can be passed on to the next custodians of the EU presidency and the subsequent phases of our shared digital public services programme.

Gar Mac Críosta is digital advisor strategy & architecture at the HSE, and co-founder of Meitheal Digiteach 2026

Having recently edited a national news magazine in Australia, I was full of thoughts. But there was one question in the advert that stumped me. What was my preferred salary?

He loved my application, he said, but there was just one thing. How wedded was I to that salary I had mentioned? “Because it’s a lot more than what I’m paid.”

At the time, I was mortified. My face burned. What an idiot I had been to name such an outlandish figure. Why hadn’t I done a better job of researching the going rate for deputy magazine editors?

I also think of how much easier it would have been if that advert had simply listed the salary on offer. That way, I would have known if it was worth my while to apply and everyone else, inside and outside the magazine, would have had a better idea of whether their pay was fair, or if they should demand more. This is, of course, precisely why so many employers do not spell out salaries in public.

For similar reasons, job hunters are often asked to disclose their salary history, even though this is an excellent way to bake in the lower pay endured by so many women, ethnic minorities and others.

Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it?

It’s tough to ask for £50,000 for a job, no matter how well qualified you are, if you have just revealed your last role paid £35,000, which it might have if you had been doing the same work at, say, a charity.

Women were told for years to just “lean in” and become savvier negotiators. Thankfully, this approach is fading as research shows the benefits of policies aimed at fixing the practice of negotiations, instead of fixing the women.

This is why the EU has brought in a directive requiring employers to do two things: tell job seekers about starting salaries or pay ranges, and stop asking them about their pay histories. A number of US states already have such measures, which can help to shrink a gender wage gap that averaged 11 per cent across OECD countries in 2023.

The deadline to put the EU directive into national law was June 2026, but unfortunately many countries have yet to get there. They include Germany, the bloc’s largest economy, where Indeed data shows that less than 15 per cent of job advertisements include explicit pay information. That number plunges for sectors such as banking and finance, which typically have far worse gender pay gaps.

No wonder thousands of women are supporting outfits such as Female X Finance, a five-year-old start-up that aims to help boost women’s careers in the financial industry. Its Dutch co-founders just published their second annual survey of the salaries – and bonuses – being paid in investment banking, M&A, private equity and other fields in the UK and the Netherlands.

HR bosses predict AI will not cause ‘significant reduction’ in employee numbers

How I wish this type of information, and those pay transparency laws, had been around when I answered that magazine advert all those years ago.

If you’re wondering, I never did get the job. It went to an insider, which is probably just as well. I’m sure they did a far better job than I would have done, but I would still like to know how much they were paid. – The Financial Times

Jame Carville’s’s famous maxim, “It’s the economy, stupid”, might need to be refined to “It’s the price economy, stupid”, to highlight what matters most to voters in the 2020s.

Trump’s political shtick has always been to proclaim everything he touches gold. It won’t wash this time.

]]><![CDATA[Musk won his battle with Swedish union but it is still business as usual]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/10/25/musk-won-his-battle-with-swedish-union-but-it-is-still-business-as-usual/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/10/25/musk-won-his-battle-with-swedish-union-but-it-is-still-business-as-usual/Sun, 25 Oct 2026 08:00:00 +0000One of my bugbears about journalists – myself included – is that we tend to pile into stories when they first develop, explain why they matter, then forget about them and move on to the next new thing. But there is value in paying attention to how stories end.

Take, for example, the battle that broke out three years ago between Elon Musk and Sweden’s trade union movement. In 2023, a group of Tesla mechanics in Sweden went on strike over their employer’s refusal to sign a collective agreement with their union, IF Metall.

Other unions joined in. They halted postal deliveries, waste collection and the unloading of cars at ports.

The stakes were high. Musk did not want to set a precedent that he would recognise unions anywhere. And Sweden’s trade unions did not want to allow Tesla to undermine the country’s labour market model, in which government regulation takes a back seat and employers and unions negotiate the rules between themselves.

Journalists flocked to cover it. Musk called it “insane”. But how did it end?

Musk won. This summer, IF Metall announced that it was calling off the strike after more than 1,000 days because Tesla had bought out all the striking members.

“Without workers on strike, there is no strike,” said Veli-Pekka Säikkälä, the collective bargaining secretary at LO, the Swedish trade union confederation, in a statement at the time.

What does it mean that Musk was victorious? For the global labour movement – and indeed anyone with ambitions to curb the power of the tech titans of our age – it is hardly encouraging that even one of the strongest trade union movements in the world could not force Tesla to the table.

After all, the Swedish unions have high membership levels, deep pockets and a supportive institutional set-up, all things that elude unions in many other countries.

In the US, for example, trade unions thought they had secured a historic victory in 2022 when workers in an Amazon warehouse in Staten Island voted to form a union. But more than four years later, Amazon has still not even negotiated a contract.

But while the “Swedish model” could not break Musk, it does not seem as if Musk has broken the Swedish model either. Although trade union officials did worry that Tesla could be the thin end of the wedge, those I spoke to on a recent visit to Stockholm took some solace from the fact that they have continued to sign collective agreements with other companies, including with tech firms that will help to shape the future of the economy.

After a year of negotiations, for example, including a strike threat, video games company King (maker of Candy Crush) signed a collective agreement with Swedish unions last month.

“The Tesla strike is important because it’s an emblematic company in the green transition – at least it was,” German Bender of the think tank Arena Idé, who wrote a book on the conflict, tells me. “But the strike ended, the union lost, and the Swedish model hasn’t crumbled.”

What if the strike had gone the other way and Musk had been the one to lose? Entering into the Swedish way of doing things could have given him an insight into a very different type of trade unionism from the American style he knows and dislikes.

Although they have become known in recent years for their fight with Tesla, in fact, Sweden has the most pro-technology trade unionists I have come across.

Susan Schurman, professor of labour studies and employment relations at Rutgers University, says that Nordic unions in general understand that it is vital for employers to remain competitive in export-led economies.

“They don’t focus on restraining technology; they focus on: ‘How do we incorporate this in a way that will help our companies remain competitive and make sure our members get their fair share of the profits?’” she tells me. “American unions have not historically thought this way.”

Indeed, the Nordic region’s powerful unions have hardly held companies back on implementing the latest tech. Sweden has been called the Silicon Valley of Europe because of its high number of start-ups.

Meanwhile, the percentage of businesses that have adopted artificial intelligence is higher in Denmark, Finland and Sweden than any other country in the OECD’s database – and well in excess of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development average.

As one Swedish trade unionist put it to me: “We don’t fear new technology. We fear old technology.” A sentiment with which Musk – were he willing to listen – would probably agree. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

Brosnan is active in the club, still playing Gaelic football, as well as soccer, and coaches junior teams. The family also enjoy life on the water. “Your best friend in Cayman is someone who owns a boat,” he says.

The family are well-settled now, and Brosnan says he cannot foresee a move back to Ireland anytime soon though he does not rule it out in the longer term. They make visits to Ireland twice a year typically.

“We’ve been away a long time at this stage, and you do miss friends and family, so we try to catch up with as many people as possible on these trips. WhatsApp is great but it’s not the same as sitting down and having a pint with someone.”

]]><![CDATA[Have Berkshire Hathaway investors really moved on from Warren Buffett?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/25/have-berkshire-hathaway-investors-really-moved-on-from-warren-buffett/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/25/have-berkshire-hathaway-investors-really-moved-on-from-warren-buffett/Sun, 25 Oct 2026 05:47:00 +0000Berkshire Hathaway shares have hit record highs, prompting a Bloomberg headline that investors have “moved on” from Warren Buffett (disclosure: I own shares in Berkshire).

But have they really?

Shares have certainly had a good run, hitting their first all-time high since May 2nd, 2025, the day before Buffett announced he was stepping down.

The rise has been rapid, with Berkshire going on a 10-day winning streak, its first since 2018. The gains came as nerves over the AI trade rattled semiconductor stocks, with Berkshire outperforming the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index by 22 percentage points in little over a fortnight.

That’s an impressive level of outperformance, but it doesn’t change the bigger picture. Since Buffett announced his impending departure 17 months ago, Berkshire shares have been essentially flat, whereas the S&P 500 advanced some 35 per cent.

The valuation story is similarly revealing. Immediately before Buffett’s announcement, Berkshire traded at about 1.8 times book value, well above its historical norm of roughly 1.4-1.5 times.

That looked generous even with Buffett still in charge. The subsequent sell-off wrung out that excess, with Berkshire trading at 1.55 times book value at the end of 2025. By March 2026 it had slipped further, to about 1.45, and it remains around that level today.

The recent rally, then, doesn’t so much suggest new-found confidence in Buffett’s successor, Greg Abel, as it does a flight to safety amid growing nerves over AI.

In fairness to Abel, nor do the figures amount to a vote of no confidence. However, if investors once paid a premium for Buffett himself, that premium is difficult to discern today.

]]>Dan Brouillette
