Poland and Vietnam have upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership, pledging to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, security and defence, as well as education, science, technology and cultural exchanges.

“Vietnam and Poland share a success story in terms of development,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a joint press conference with his Vietnamese counterpart Lê Minh Hưng in Hanoi on Monday. “The time has come to turn our successes into joint actions that will open up more opportunities.”

The announcement comes amid a broader flurry of Polish diplomacy in Asia, with Tusk arriving in Hanoi following a visit to India and President Karol Nawrocki visiting the Philippines earlier this month. Poland also recently signed new strategic agreements with South Korea and Japan.

🇵🇱🤝🇻🇳 Polska i Wietnam wchodzą na poziom partnerstwa strategicznego!

✅ Podczas wizyty w Hanoi premier @donaldtusk oraz szef wietnamskiego rządu Lê Minh Hưng podjęli decyzję o podniesieniu wzajemnych relacji do rangi partnerstwa strategicznego, otwierając nowy rozdział we… pic.twitter.com/CCvHmc3eva

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 26, 2026

Tusk, who was making the first visit by a Polish prime minister to Vietnam in 16 years, pointed to the two countries’ rapid recent economic development.

“Within a single generation, Vietnam achieved middle-income status”, while “Poland recently joined the ranks of the world’s 20 largest economies”.

In fact, while Poland was forecast to join the world’s 20 largest economies last year, it eventually fell narrowly short. However, it is expected to soon overtake Switzerland, the current holder of 20th place.

Tusk said that, during his visit, he had often heard people say that “Poland is the Vietnam of Europe and Vietnam is the Poland of Asia”.

Last year, Hưng’s predecessor, Phạm Minh Chính, became the first Vietnamese prime minister in 15 years to visit Poland.

The two countries first established diplomatic relations in 1950, and both leaders emphasised Poland’s large Vietnamese community, which dates back to students arriving around that time.

Speaking on Monday, Hưng noted the two countries’ strong traditional ties, adding that Vietnam always remembers and is grateful for Polish support and assistance during his country’s struggle for independence and national reunification, reports the Vietnamese News Agency (VNA).

The Vietnamese are Poland's largest non-European migrant group.

Photographer Zula Rabikowska, through her images and interviews, offers an insight into their experiences, identities and the challenges they face https://t.co/tsRwHINapQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 27, 2019

The new strategic partnership agreement signed by Tusk and Hưng pledges to “bring tangible benefits to both nations and contribute to peace, stability, cooperation and prosperity”.

It contains commitments to “maintain regular high-level contacts”, reduce non-tariff barriers to trade, and strengthen cooperation on defence, including trade in military equipment.

On Sunday, Poland’s deputy minister for state assets, Konrad Gołota, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that negotiations are already underway for Vietnam to buy Polish Krab howitzers and Rosomak armoured fighting vehicles, among other hardware.

Polish arms firm Mesko has announced the best financial results in its 100-year history.

Record revenues and profits were driven in large part by international demand for Mesko's flagship Piorun air-defence system, which has proved successful in Ukraine https://t.co/Dx1yY54qCP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026

Tusk, pointing to Poland’s current trade deficit with Vietnam, said that Warsaw’s “priority remains a better balance in trade”.

“The sectors in which the Vietnamese side is most interested, and in which we really have something to offer, are the arms industry, satellite and space cooperation, pharmaceuticals and food, especially dairy products,” he added.

Tusk also announced that the number of annual Polish-Vietnamese student exchanges would rise by 250% and noted that Poland’s national carrier, LOT, would resume direct Warsaw-Hanoi flights in the first quarter of 2027.

Poland is taking steps to attract more foreign students as universities face lower enrollment due to demographic decline.

Turkey, South Korea, Vietnam and Uzbekistan are among the countries with which the government is cultivating stronger academic ties https://t.co/r878KqS5OV

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2026

The Polish prime minister acknowledged differences between Poland and Vietnam’s approach to Russia’s war in Ukraine. Vietnam, which has long maintained close ties with Moscow, has avoided condemning the Russian invasion.

But he emphasised his belief that, “because of their history, wartime experience and international relations, both Vietnam and Poland can contribute a great deal to the peace process”.

Tusk’s trip to Vietnam follows a three-day visit to India, where he and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030.

Poland and India's PMs have, after meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies

Polish-Indian relations are "gaining speed", said @narendramodi https://t.co/iIVIkCXnvr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 22, 2026

In April, Tusk visited South Korea, upgrading Poland’s relations with the country he described as Poland’s “most important ally after the United States”, and deepened Poland’s strategic partnership with Japan on the same tour.

Earlier this month, Tusk also announced plans to visit China before the end of the year. Meanwhile, President Nawrocki visited the Philippines this month as part of a bid to secure backing from Asian nations for Poland’s hoped-for membership in the G20.

Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week.

The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki.

🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026

In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health.

In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases.

 

A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion.

The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%).

The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority).

One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand.

In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023

The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”.

Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”.

Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026

In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition.

However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law.

By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here)

Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now.

No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September.

He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government.

The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border.

However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024

Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision.

The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy.

Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week.

The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland.

 

Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out.

Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves.

Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”.

Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII.

On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024

This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship.

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions.

In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning.

Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago.

Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland.

If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation.

This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands.

Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute.

Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims

Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken.

As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful.

But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance.

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, came to power in December 2023, it pledged to liberalise the abortion laws after eight years of rule by the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party.

In particular, it wanted to reverse the 2020 TK ruling, which outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means abortions can now only take place in two cases: where the pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health.

 

However, in the almost three years since, the government has failed to introduce any new legislation on abortion. One effort to do so in 2024 collapsed amid disagreements between more conservative and liberal elements of Tusk’s coalition.

Finally, earlier this week, the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, approved two abortion bills: one that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling; the other that would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, those measures do not go far enough for many of those attending Tuesday’s protests, who are seeking abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

In any case, both bills approved by the Sejm are likely to be blocked by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of government bills. Nawrocki has made his opposition to abortion clear.

Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did.

They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises.

The hospital scandal

Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk.

In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients.

Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services.

KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors.

Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens.

The cryptocurrency scandal

The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds.

However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm.

Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026

For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro.

The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto).

For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations.

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026

PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation.

Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive.

The diminishing impact of scandals

It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape.

For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party.

A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force.

Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions.

 

The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland.

Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence.

Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage.

Scandal-neutralising structural shifts

This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics.

Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy.

Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative.

Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals

The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023

This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage.

Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines.

In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media.

So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high.

How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment.

Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity.

They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues.

Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion

Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments.

Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence.

The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote.

In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day.

Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections.

We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025

And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed.

Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them.

Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote.

So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.

Wewiór warned that, while the Ukrainian and Polish governments have recently made progress towards reconciliation over historical issues, “irresponsible local activists are damaging these relations by honouring people clearly responsible for crimes and collaborating with the Nazis”.

The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”.

Mamy to! Sejm przyjął dwa projekty: dekryminalizujący pomocnictwo w aborcji i przywracający aborcyjny kompromis.
To niezbędne minimum i pierwszy krok.
Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC

— Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.

However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.

One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.

That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.

The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.

 

In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).

Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.

Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to allow abortions when a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.

However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.

All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to decriminalise abortion assistance (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.

Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Mon, 26 Oct 2026 20:14:15 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Does the government realise the rich aren’t leaving on a whim? https://www.cityam.com/does-the-government-realise-the-rich-arent-leaving-on-a-whim/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 04:46:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471321

From experience advising high net worth individuals, the “exodus of wealth” is rarely a decision taken lightly, writes Yorke Eaton.]]>

From experience advising high net worth individuals, the “exodus of wealth” is rarely a decision taken lightly, writes Yorke Eaton 

Much has been reported about the departure of wealthy individuals from the UK and the impact this will have on tax revenues. A recent analysis suggested that ultra-high net worth residents collectively worth £121bn have either left or loosened their ties to the UK in recent years. Tax changes and uncertainty about what’s to come have often been cited as factors behind the trend.

From experience advising high net worth individuals, the “exodus of wealth” is rarely a decision taken lightly. For anyone seriously entertaining the idea, the process tends to begin months, or even years, before anyone boards a plane. And, contrary to popular opinion, it is not always the tax they face today that leads wealthy families to relocate overseas; it also tends to be the uncertainty over what their bill will be in the future.

The benefit of affluent individuals and families to the UK isn’t just the tax they pay. It is the money they spend and invest here, the people they employ and the knock-on benefits for tax revenues and consumer spending.

So, how do we retain high net worth individuals? The government needs to understand what might prompt UK residents to consider becoming non-resident and provide a compelling answer to why they should remain.

The UK has an enormous amount going for it and many wealthy families want to live here for personal, family and business reasons. The opportunity is to provide sufficient stability and certainty for them to make long-term decisions here with confidence.

HNWIs are looking for certainty

In its submission ahead of the Autumn Budget, TheCityUK makes a compelling case for a tax roadmap and simplification of the regime to support growth and competitiveness. 

The government may also wish to review its recent changes to Business and Agricultural Relief for inheritance tax purposes, with a view to a system that better targets the behaviours the changes were designed to address, while allowing genuine business owners to invest knowing that the business can continue after their death. Various credible alternatives have been discussed within the tax industry.

The UK is currently one of the only major European countries without a favourable regime to encourage the internationally mobile affluent to make the UK home.

The UK could look to schemes such as those Greece and Italy have put in place to attract internationally mobile affluent people to invest in the UK and make it their home. Leaders in the tax field have already worked on a suitable Investor Visa structure and recent reports suggest this is something the government is now considering. Where people choose to live depends heavily on their circumstances. Age, family make-up and what people want for their children all play a part. For some, this is about their own residence in the relatively near term. For others, the concern is much further ahead: ensuring what they have spent years building can continue to provide for future generations.

There is no room for complacency. Traditionally, children’s schooling has been one of the barriers to wealthy families leaving the UK. Yet this is being made easier by the growing number of prestigious UK school brands opening in favourable tax jurisdictions.

Becoming non-resident is a major personal and financial decision, and many won’t leave even if there is a significant financial advantage in doing so.

The challenge for the Treasury is to understand what influences these decisions and what can be done to encourage wealth to remain in the UK. The numbers tell us what has already happened; announcements in the Budget and conversations in the coming months will determine what comes next.

Yorke Eaton is head of private wealth at Addleshaw Goddard

Geoffrey Howe sipped a gin and tonic, Nigel Lawson quaffed a wine spritzer, while George Osborne and Gordon Brown stuck to mineral water. Ahead of his first Budget, one of the many decisions weighing on Chancellor John Healey’s mind will be whether to get a little squiffy at the despatch box.

If he does, it could be an early signal of what lies in Healey’s red box. The Chancellor has made much of his love for ale, and pub industry lobbyists are watching to see whether he brings a pint with him on Wednesday. The thought process is that if the Chancellor delivers the Budget nursing a beer, he won’t hike costs on the pub industry while doing it.

The hospitality sector is in a unique position ahead of this week’s Budget: the main tax cut they had been hoping for has already been announced. Just days into his premiership, Andy Burnham unveiled a 20 per cent cut to the business rates bill paid by pubs, clubs and music venues. 

Burnham, who used his first photo-op as PM to get a round in at the Hare, a McMullen’s pub in Harlow, said the move would protect pubs, which he called “the beating heart of our communities,” adding that the tax cut was “just the start.”

Burnham was right to acknowledge that this tax cut was not the end of it, hospitality industry figures said, though they suggested pub companies are getting their hopes up that any more substantial support will come out of this Budget. 

The industry has urged the government to reform the business rates system for good – a pledge in Labour’s election manifesto – and help employers curb the rising number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet). 

With Healey set to deliver a “steady-as-she-goes Budget” in a bid to restore the UK’s fiscal credibility, hospitality figures have accepted that these issues will not be solved in one session at the despatch box. 

But this hasn’t stopped some pub bosses calling for another round. Some in the industry hope for an increase to tax breaks for draught beer, which the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA) says could create 7,100 jobs, including 3,400 for workers under 25, and knock 10p off the price of a pint.

Chris Jowsey, chief executive of Legal & General-owned Admiral Taverns, which runs about 1,350 pubs in the UK, said the beer duty paid by British landlords is among the highest in Europe. “With costs continuing to rise and many pubs working hard to simply keep their doors open, there is often little choice but to pass the cost on to customers,” he said.

VAT is ‘elephant in the room’

Freezing beer duty and increasing the draught discount, so beer served on tap is liable for less tax, from 13.9 to 30 per cent, would “give pubs much-needed breathing space,” Jowsey said. 

Luke White, managing director of the UK arm of Estrella brewer Damm, said a freeze to beer duty would “help pubs manage the continued pressure on their margins, keep pints affordable and give businesses greater confidence to invest and plan for the future”. 

Action on beer duty at the Budget would leave a bitter taste for some pub bosses, who claim that the real way to slash hospitality costs is a cut to VAT. A campaign led by celebrity chef Tom Kerridge has been pushing for the current 20 per cent rate to be halved. 

Sir Tim Martin, chairman of JD Wetherspoon, has long bemoaned the premium punters pay for pints at pubs compared to supermarkets. He claims cutting VAT could give pubs a leg-up by drawing more punters away from Sainsbury’s and Tesco.

“Reductions in beer duty and business rates would be warmly welcomed, but VAT is the elephant in the room,” Sir Tim said. The Wetherspoon boss said he will also be on the lookout for “sleight of hand” increases to pubs’ costs at the Budget, including hikes to sugar taxes or climate levies. 

While Burnham’s business rates cut was welcomed, some pub landlords still haven’t forgiven Labour for the hikes to their tax bills that followed last year’s Budget. 

Andy Lennox, who led hundreds of pubs in barring Labour MPs from their premises late last year, said a change to beer duty would be “completely and utterly the wrong thing to do”. The sector needs a cut to VAT and any other tax changes billed as a boost for pubs are “all just noise,” he said. 

While pub landlords would toast the sight of John Healey clutching a pint of ale at the Budget on Wednesday, they will hope his efforts to revive Britain’s hospitality industry are not all froth.

Amir Khan’s trade union for combat sports, the Global Fighters’ Association, has hired top barrister Jonathan Caplan KC to lead an investigation into boxing and MMA. The GFA is aiming to raise £500,000 through crowdfunding to complete its certification as a union and launch the three-month inquiry into the safety, governance and treatment of fighters [...]]]>

Amir Khan’s trade union for combat sports, the Global Fighters’ Association, has hired top barrister Jonathan Caplan KC to lead an investigation into boxing and MMA.

The GFA is aiming to raise £500,000 through crowdfunding to complete its certification as a union and launch the three-month inquiry into the safety, governance and treatment of fighters in all combat sports.

Caplan, whose hourly rate for legal work is more than £500, is regarded as an expert on health and safety and regulatory justice inquiries, and will produce a report setting out what changes are needed to give fighters the same protections and rights as other athletes.

“Over the last decade or so, professional sports such as rugby, football and horse racing have raised their game when it comes to the welfare of the participants,” said GFA chair designate Simon Bazalgette. 

“They recognise that the brand of the sport increasingly depends on demonstrating that best-in-class welfare underpins any aspiration to grow the audience and the commercial value of the sport. 

“It is striking that combat sport is one of the last workplaces with no professional representation for its workers, meaning little protection, no minimum health and safety standard, no independent pension scheme, no insurance floor, and no single body a fighter can turn to when something goes wrong. 

“The GFA has been formed to rectify this, to help the sport create a stronger bond of trust with its participants and its audience, and thereby give a stronger foundation for growth.”

Ali Act moves ‘should be wake-up call’ for combat sports

British boxers Khan and Paul Smith set up the GFA in 2022 in response to concerns that fighters lacked protections against financial and health and safety risks. 

Their latest move comes amid efforts to amend the Ali Act in the US, which was established to afford more rights to combat sports participants. 

“What’s happening to the Ali Act in the US right now should be a wake-up call for every combat sport worker, everywhere,” said GFA Acting General Secretary Paul Maloney.

“It’s the one piece of legislation anywhere in the world that gives fighters a level of workplace protection, and it’s currently being rewritten in a way critics say favours the promoters and networks that already hold most of the power. 

“If it can be stripped back there, it can happen anywhere else that lacks its own independent, respected voice for fighters – which is exactly why the GFA exists.”

The Chancellor has been warned that the “dam is starting to break” on surging shop price inflation, which retailers had kept at bay with heavy discounting.

Shop prices rose by 2.1 per cent in the year to October, according to new data from the British Retail Consortium, ahead of September’s 1.4 per cent and the three-month average of 1.6 per cent. 

Retailers have said the long-feared spike in inflation caused by the Iran war’s knock-on effects on energy and supply costs is beginning to take hold. 

Rising prices of long-life goods are behind this uplift. Fresh food inflation remained steady at 2.6 per cent, while overall food prices rose 2.9 per cent in the year to October, up from 2.5 per cent the previous month. 

Price inflation among non-food goods almost doubled, from 0.8 per cent in September to 1.7 per cent in the year to this month. 

Shortly following the US and Israel’s first strikes on Iran, food industry experts warned that the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz would cause food prices in the UK to surge, as they did following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

The Food and Drink Federation (FDF) had tipped food inflation to surge by as much as 10 per cent by the end of this year, but later adjusted its forecast to eye up a peak of 6.4 per cent by next summer.

Chancellor urged to slash costs on retailers

Food inflation has remained steady at 1.3 per cent in recent months, prompting bosses at top supermarkets, including Sainsbury’s and Tesco, to question whether these cost increases would pass through.

Mike Watkins, head of retailer insight at data firm NIQ, said retailers had managed to delay some of the impact of these price rises by working hard to discount products.

“High street retailers, faced with consumers becoming more cautious in the face of higher energy and fuel costs, will now be more reliant on promotions to drive discretionary non-food spend,” he said. 

Helen Dickinson, the BRC’s chief executive, said: “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years.

“The message to the Chancellor ahead of tomorrow’s Budget could not be clearer: act now or prices will keep on rising. Without a change of course, October’s jump in inflation is only the beginning.”

The trade body has urged Chancellor John Healey to follow a “simple recipe” to halt food inflation, including cancelling hikes to business rates, slashing the cost of employment, and ditching costly packaging taxes.

]]> 2471474Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong ‘You can walk in the road!’: Inside Oxford Street’s first day without traffic https://www.cityam.com/you-can-walk-in-the-road-inside-oxford-streets-first-day-without-traffic/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 20:13:25 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471578

As the first phase of the mayor's Oxford Street pedestrianisation project began, Anna Moloney rushed to Selfridges to soak up the scene.]]>

The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street felt like the dream that could never come true, but this morning the first phase of the mayor’s transformation project began. Anna Moloney rushed to Selfridges to soak up the first day atmosphere

It’s only day one of Oxford Street’s pedestrianisation, but its place as a pivotal moment in the history of the street is already being memorialised. In the middle of the newly cordoned-off stretch, I stop to read a series of museum exhibit-style boards, narrating the history of the road from the Romans to today: “Long before Oxford Street became London’s busiest shopping street, and ahead of its transformation into a traffic-free space,” the chronicle begins – harking back, then, to all of yesterday.

It’s a confident launch for the long-mooted and highly contested project (possibly rushed through to give Sadiq Khan his legacy project), but if the mood of shoppers on the street is anything to go by, it’s already going down as a success. 

A celebratory atmosphere

Indeed, as I proceed past the first batch of neon-green bollards signalling the start of the traffic-free zone, the mood is decisively celebratory. “You can walk in the road!” one balding Brit exclaims, springing from the pavement to the tarmac. Elsewhere, despite the drizzle, almost everyone is snapping pictures, while a number even stop to pose in front of the bollards. Two women, wanting to document the moment together, interrupt a security worker to take their photograph, while further up I spot a row of six men, hands soberly clasped in front of them, poised for their picture of this momentous day. 

Pepe Velo, a wine importer for Spain who I interrupt taking a picture of the bollards on his way to a meeting, says he thinks it’s a great initiative. “It’s extremely difficult with the amount of people to go shopping with just two pavements, my wife and I always end up travelling up the middle,” he tells me, referring to the islands that stand between some of the traffic on the street. Further up the street I come by Daniel Te, a young artist perched on one of the street’s shiny new green benches, sketching the car-free scene ahead of him. “I love a good pedestrianised street, it’s so crazy to see no cars here,” he says, adding that he would definitely be more likely to come shopping on Oxford Street now. “I do find myself intuitively staying on the pavements though,” he laughs, and indeed it is notable as I stroll along that the crowding is still concentrated at the edges, presumably out of habit as everyone gets used to the novelty of walking slap bang down the middle.

Aside from the biggie – no traffic – the transformation of the street design-wise is still in its early stages, and no doubt some will be determined to scoff at the opening as a damp squib compared with the sunny, tree-lined scenes promised by the shiny renderings pumped out by the mayor’s office. Currently, it’s just the Orchard Street to Great Portland Street stretch marked off (the Selfridges end), though further extensions are in the works, and the current trial period will seek to identify and mitigate potential issues.

The Oxford Street naysayers

Naturally, removing traffic from one of London’s busiest thoroughfares does not come without downsides. When I approach one security woman stationed by the bollards to ask about her role in this pedestrianised utopia, she barks the reply: “We’re doing HMVs”. When I ask what HVMs are, she looks at me like I’m an idiot before a three-word explanation: hostile vehicle mitigation. 

Another key job of the security personnel is scolding cyclists. I watch one flag down a Deliveroo driver, who proceeds to dismount his bike, walk a few steps, and promptly get back on again.

Cabbies, too, are not happy about the change. One taxi driver tells me through his window that today, a half-term Monday, should have been the easiest day for the change, yet it was “already carnage” down the side roads. He says he’s keeping his fingers crossed the initiative will be reversed. 

A key driver of the project has been to give London’s retailers a shot in the arm by rejuvenating the city’s flagship high street. A worker at the big Boots tells me it’s been a little bit busier today already, though the rain was partially driving more people to shelter inside anyway. A worker at a nearby shoe shop tells me she thinks the surge will come next week, when more people realise the change has happened, but says she’s not excited about it – she doesn’t want it any busier before Christmas.

She may then wish to consider a job at one of the many vape or tackier souvenir shops that populate the street, and that Sadiq Khan has expressed a particular distaste for. When I go into one such establishment to ask if they are excited about the change, the manager says not. He says business has been completely dead today, which he attributes to the lack of buses. For the mayor, who has said he wishes to see the loss of Oxford Street’s “dross” shops as a result of the change, that may well be a victory.

With days to go until John Healey delivers a Budget expected to target banks with a cash raid, Samuel Norman looks at the UK bank tax framework and other experiments across Europe. 

For years City lobbyists managed to bat away demands for a bank tax hike. As Chancellor, despite delivering two tax-heavy Budgets, Rachel Reeves successfully saw off a clamour from her own backbenches to target the sector.

But under Andy Burnham’s government and John Healey’s Treasury, times have changed. Analysts now expect a raid on the banks to be the base case in Wednesday’s Budget – and the City is bracing for impact.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM, told City AM an increase to the bank levy was “probably the most likely option”. He added, depending on the remnants of Healey’s fiscal headroom and spending commitments, it may be the only major tax-raising measure introduced in the Budget.

The UK banking sector paid a record £47.8bn into Treasury coffers in the year to April 2026, according to a report from trade body UK Finance. The industry already faces a raft of different levies, from the typical employment tax to sector-specific charges.

These include the UK banking levy, an annual tax on balance sheet liabilities, and a three per cent surcharge on corporation tax.

The two taxes are expected to have generated around £2.6bn for the Treasury purse in the last year, according to PwC analysis. The total bank tax contribution is expected to be around 4.3 per cent of government tax receipts.

How far Healey seeks to push ahead with a tax increase will depend on his political appetite as much as the fiscal crunch he is faces. 

Some campaigners have urged the Chancellor to maximise the opportunity and opt for a windfall tax on the booming profits of the largest institutions. But it is a tried and tested experiment across Europe – and in some cases, it may give rise to caution. 

Trial and error 

Italy attempted an aggressive 40 per cent levy on its banking sector back in 2023 following interest rate hikes from the European central bank. 

A coalition government led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said banks would be taxed on net interest income earned in 2022 or 2023 that exceeded the prior years’ baselines by five to 10 per cent. It was expected to raise up to €3bn (£2.5bn) but would go on to raise …almost nothing. 

Markets were caught off guard by the initial announcement, sending bank stocks plummeting. Italy’s banking index dropped nearly eight per cent in a single day after news emerged, wiping out billions from valuations and panicking investors. 

Facing fierce lobbying, the government added an opt-out clause where banks could avoid the tax entirely if they kept 2.5 times their tax bill locked on their balance sheets as capital reserves instead of paying it out to shareholders. 

Nearly all major banks – including Unicredit and the country’s biggest by total assets, Intesa Sanpaolo – opted to build up their reserves. It gave the government some political points, allowing it to claim it took on big banks and forced them to strengthen the financial system, but the initial tax plan proved to be a colossal misfire.

In a more moderate instance, Spain introduced a 4.8 per cent levy on banks’ net interest income and fee revenues for 2023 and 2024. Pedro Sánchez’s government left no loopholes and succeeded in raising €1.3bn in 2023 and €1.7bn in 2024. The levy hit banks earning over €800m, which left a majority of smaller lenders and international banks outside the target range. 

The levy was originally planned to be a two-year tax but the government would later extend it to 2027 and replaced the flat 4.8 per cent with a sliding scale between one to seven per cent tied to revenue earned. 

While more successful than Italy’s bank tax bid, Spain faced harsh consequences. Top banks Santander and BBVA adamantly fought the tax. The initial announcement in mid-2022 wiped some €5bn off the value of Spanish banking stocks and triggered a wave of legal rows. It also tightened lending criteria for risky borrowers and restricted credit growth as lenders adapted to the increased cost.

Tax to spend 

Both Italy and Spain framed their taxes under a patriotic mandate, to help cushion households against soaring inflation and rising living costs.

Lithuania introduced a bank tax in 2023 after it faced an eerily similar scenario to John Healey with a significant funding gap for defence. The government launched the ‘Temporary Solidary Contribution’ marking the introduction of one of the most uniquely focused windfall tax models across Europe.

It took the form of a 60 per cent rate applied to net interest income that exceeded a 40 per cent jump over the bank’s average net interest income from the previous four years. It followed rising interest rates, causing half-year profits across commercial banks to grow 150 per cent in the first half of 2023. 

The government legally restricted the tax revenue to the state defence fund and military infrastructure. It brought in over €240m in its first full year and €220m the year following, a major sum relative to the size of its economy. 

The highly concentrated nature of Lithuania’s banking sector – where three Scandinavian institutions control nearly 90 per cent of the market – made the tax simple to monitor and left incumbent lenders unable to simply pick up and leave without surrendering valuable market share.

Comparatively, in the UK the biggest five players control around 80 per cent of the deposits, but a thriving middle layer exists. Challenger institutions, building societies, and digital-first banks, such as Nationwide, Virgin Money, Monzo, and Starling, offer viable switching alternatives, ramping up competition. 

Healey has kept tight-lipped on the scope of a bank tax, telling industry bosses only of the fiscal “challenges” the country faces. But if Europe’s misfires prove anything, it is that squeezing the banks is rarely straightforward. How much he leans on the industry will depend on how deep those fiscal holes run – and how much political heat he can take.

The City of London was changed forever by a sweeping package of deregulation in 1986, known as the Big Bang. Forty years on – and facing existential threats – can the Square Mile reinvent itself again?

When Alasdair Haynes left work as a young options trader on Friday 24th October 1986, he didn’t know what world would await him when he returned on Monday morning.

For months technicians had been wiring up futuristic-looking machines in offices around the Square Mile. Haynes’s bosses had been running practice sessions on new electronic trading systems and briefing staff as best they could in preparation for the sweeping change ahead. The reality, he says, was more drastic than anyone could have imagined.

“Everybody thought on Friday that there would be a few people off the [stock exchange] trading floor working in offices, and everybody else would come in. But we came in and the trading floor was practically a desert,” Haynes, who went on to found challenger stock exchange Aquis, tells City AM. 

“Everybody else had gone off on Friday, never to come back ever again. It was a mind-blowing experience.”

On that Monday, 27th October 1986, the sudden deregulation of financial markets known as the Big Bang took effect, transforming the City of London and catapulting Britain’s financial industry into the modern age. 

The bustle and life of the London Stock Exchange floor were swapped for the screen-based Stock Exchange Automated Quotation system. Strict rules dividing work between brokers – who bought and sold shares on behalf of clients – and jobbers – who made markets and held shares – were ditched. Fixed commissions were abolished, allowing transaction fees to be negotiated freely, as were rules prohibiting international firms from owning London’s stockbrokers.

International firms piled into the City and consolidated London’s fractured broking market. Americans arrived in droves – and with them came their hard-charging, cut-throat ways of working. The City’s clubby and cosy ways were changed forever. 

“In the morning of the old days at the London Stock Exchange, you used to walk around the boxes around the edge of the exchange, and talk to everybody and find out what they thought about the market,” Haynes says. 

“You’d meet people after work in the Arbitrager or Greens, or go out to lunch. All that changed, literally as if somebody turned a light switch off.”

Speaking at the Lord Mayor’s banquet two weeks after the changes took effect, even Margaret Thatcher acknowledged her reforms were a death knell to a certain way of life.

“The new technology does have a disadvantage: the people who are making deals need never meet,” she said. “You can’t look a computer in the eye and shake its hand to close a bargain.”

The train timetables shifted too to accommodate the earlier starts and longer hours of new international arrivals coming in from the home counties, Sir Philip Augar writes in his book the Death of Gentlemanly Capitalism.

The result though was a sudden rise in jobs in Britain’s financial services sector. In early 1986, the City employed around 1m people. By 1990 that had swelled to 1.18m, according to government figures.

The deregulation drive, ushered in by Thatcher and Chancellor Nigel Lawson, triggered an explosion of activity in the Square Mile and thrust London back to the forefront of global finance. A string of huge privatisations of state-owned utilities added to a sudden influx of investment and jobs in the Square Mile.

While the day itself delivered a shot in the arm, London’s markets had been internationalising for years prior thanks to the rise of the Eurodollar market – the global banking market for dollar deposits held in banks outside the United States – and the abolition of exchange controls in 1979, which ended strict limits on moving money in and out of the country.

Duncan Weldon, the financial historian and author of Two Hundred Years of Muddling Through, argues those changes were just as significant as the sudden overhaul on that Monday in October 1986.

“The City was in this sort of funk from the 1920s, all the way up to the 1950s. And then in the 50s, ’60s and ’70s you see this rebirth in international finance in London in debt markets, because of the Eurodollar market,” he says. 

Dropping exchange controls in 1979 too was “just as big a deal as the changes to the market structure in the mid-80s”, he adds.

Big Bang 2.0?

Politicians have for years nostalgically invoked the Big Bang to pledge another wave of quick and transformative deregulation. Jeremy Hunt, Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss and Kwasi Kwarteng all promised various forms of Big Bang 2.0, claiming that slackened solvency buffers for insurance firms and an overhaul of listing rules would thrust London back to the centre of global finance.

But Weldon says the reality is more complex.

“Rhetorically, the idea of the Big Bang, and the idea there are some regulatory levers you can pull and it will turbocharge your financial sector, is clearly a very appealing one to policy makers,” he adds.

“But it helps to put this in a longer context. It wasn’t just that the policy unit in Number 10, and Nigel Lawson as Chancellor, did these reforms and it turbocharged the financial sector in London.”

Weldon’s warnings point to the challenge now facing the City as it is battered by a wave of foreign takeovers and a historic dearth of initial public offerings. While there have been signs of life for London’s listing market in recent weeks, a slew of reforms made to the rules governing UK capital markets have so far failed to yield a meaningful uptick in deals.

Changes to the buffers of insurance firms and calls for pension funds to pump more cash into domestic equities are also yet to shift the dial on domestic investment.

Policymakers and regulators point to a retreat of domestic capital as among the primary reasons for London’s market malaise. Just four per cent of the domestic stock market is now held by UK pension funds, down from 39 per cent around 20 years ago, according to think tank New Financial. Like the rebirth of the City in the 1980s, that trend has been decades in the marking.

Steven Fine, boss of City investment bank Peel Hunt, says: “The problem we’ve got is that the IPO Market hasn’t come back, and the bigger problem we’ve got is the almost complete lack of domestic demand and the hollowing out of the domestic asset management industry.

“That I think is something that is more in need of [another] Big Bang than regulatory change for listed companies.”

Few are looking at the Budget on Wednesday as a moment likely to deliver solutions and reignite the City’s animal spirits. Banks are set to be hit with higher taxes despite warnings from international bosses that such a move will force them to reallocate capital away from the UK. While a capital gains tax hike has been ruled out, the City’s calls for an end to stamp duty on shares and tax breaks for domestic investment from pension funds look set to be unheeded.

Is another Big Bang possible? Not in Haynes’s view. Rather than search for another deregulatory transformation to revive the Square Mile’s former glory, he says policymakers should learn from the principles that inspired it.

“There’s no magic wand, but the Big Bang wasn’t a magic wand. It was thought through for a long time beforehand” he says.

“It was about many things which a strong, powerful government at the time was able to push through. And that is what we need today. It’s not Big Bang 2.0 – you can’t electronify something again. But what you can do is take the same principles to make it work better.”

The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street is the most radical project to hit the West End in decades. The greening of Oxford Street, with plenty of opportunity for people to sit down and relax are both a large part of the plans. What Khan is describing is a vision of a public realm where it is anticipated that people will enjoy the new space, stay longer and spend more.

More than a shopping street

Here is the thing many people miss: Oxford Street is no longer just a shopping street. The Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, sees a wider prize. “Revitalising Oxford Street will help to super-charge regeneration, boosting jobs and economic growth in the capital and beyond,” he said. Today, Oxford Street begins to find out.

A good tax system isn’t just about raising revenue, it’s about encouraging the behaviours (working, saving, investing) that create a prosperous economy, writes Harry Bell

With the UK’s public finances up for scrutiny at the Autumn Budget, it seems the main remedy to Healey’s diminishing fiscal headroom is one that is tried, but not necessarily true: taxing the rich. However, before we look for more ways to tax wealth, we need to make sure we aren’t discouraging people from creating it in the first place. 

If we want a prosperous economy, we need people to work, save, invest, build businesses and take risks. People understand the need to pay tax, but there needs to be a reward for playing an active and productive role in boosting the country, rather than a penalty. Tax policy doesn’t just raise revenue, it changes behaviour. The government needs to think much harder about what behaviours they are encouraging, particularly when it comes to individual, isolated taxes. 

Pensions are a good example. People need to be encouraged to save for their retirement, especially when there is evidence that many aren’t saving enough. In fact, our latest research shows that one in six (16 per cent) mass-affluent Brits have either completely or temporarily stopped contributing to their pension, while nine per cent don’t have one at all. Continually changing the rules will make people question whether pensions will still be attractive in 20 or 30 years, which is a terrible long-term strategy. 

A case study: Capital Gains Tax

Capital Gains Tax (CGT) also shows why behaviour matters. A future increase might initially bring disposals forward and create a bump in tax receipts, but what happens afterwards? People can simply choose not to sell. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) specifically recognises both bringing disposals forward and “locking in” gains by delaying disposals, potentially even until death, as behavioural responses to capital taxes. The economy will not benefit from a tax system where the tax-efficient decision is simply to do nothing.

The same goes for entrepreneurs, and the government needs to be encouraging people to take risks, build businesses and employ people. Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) has already become less generous, with the applicable CGT rate rising to 18 per cent from April 2026. A significant increase in CGT without appropriate consideration of BADR could seriously damage the incentive to build, and ultimately sell, a business.

The government should also address some of the strange tax traps in place, and resist the urge to introduce anymore, or push people into higher bands. The loss of the personal allowance above £100,000 means someone can face a very high effective marginal rate over a relatively narrow band of earnings, while the High Income Child Benefit Charge creates another taper for families. People should be incentivised to work hard, progress and reap some of the rewards, rather than trying to fall under arbitrary points where earning the next pound suddenly becomes far less worthwhile. 

More broadly, the tax system is so complicated and intertwined that changing one thing can have consequences elsewhere. CGT interacts with inheritance tax, pensions and estate planning, for example. The Treasury needs to look at the system as a whole and the ripple effect that could occur due to a singular change, rather than treating taxpayers as passive entries on a spreadsheet.

It’s widely understood that a good tax system raises revenue, but it should also encourage the behaviours that create a prosperous economy: working, saving, investing and building businesses, and ultimately, reaping the rewards of doing all those things. 

Harry Bell is director of financial planning at Raymond James

Proponents of the measure argue that higher sector taxes have merits on grounds of fairness. Banks have done well due to macroeconomic factors and they must pay their share when people are struggling.

And it cannot be fair that banks, which already face higher taxes than their competitors in Amsterdam and Frankfurt – and nearly 20 per cent more than our closest competitor as a financial centre, New York – are expected to shoulder an even greater burden.

Should the Chancellor announce this damaging step, the effects will not only be felt in the City of London, but in every town and city in the UK. Greater Manchester, which the Prime Minister wants to form into the UK’s second political and economic centre, hosts 59,000 of these jobs.

Government should be looking to expand this contribution, instead it risks diminishing it.

Removing this tax would help strengthen the case for UK listings, supporting a wider ecosystem of high-paying jobs in legal, advisory and accounting services, while giving British businesses better access to the capital they need to grow.

This is progress we must build on, not put at risk. Forty years after the Big Bang helped transform London’s financial markets, the Chancellor has an opportunity to strengthen the conditions for investment and growth for decades to come. We should not risk harming the goose that lays the golden egg.
