The post Bedrock Robotics nears $1B in total funding as demand for autonomous heavy equipment surges appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Bedrock Robotics automates large excavators to improve construction site economics. | Credit: Bedrock Robotics

San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics has raised $600 million in Series C funding, co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital, at a $4.1 billion valuation. The round brings its total funding to nearly $1 billion as it scales fully autonomous heavy equipment to address nationwide construction labor shortages.

The round included new investors US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT), Bessemer Venture Partners, and Temasek, alongside existing investors 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital, NVIDIA, and others. Bedrock said this will accelerate the deployment of Bedrock-equipped machines across commercial construction sites across the U.S., helping contractors use existing heavy equipment more safely, predictably, and at greater capacity.

The new capital follows a rapid commercial expansion beyond the company’s initial footprint in the West and Central South into the Midwest and South Atlantic. Anchored by a major partnership with Southwest contractor Haydon to automate earthwork in Texas, Bedrock has added regional partners across Minnesota, Florida, Georgia, Missouri, and Virginia—pushing its autonomous retrofits onto live job sites spanning data centers, healthcare facilities, and heavy civil infrastructure.

“We have proven that fully autonomous excavators can perform real work of value alongside the crews and workflows already in place on job sites,” said Boris Sofman, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Robotics. “The next challenge is delivering that capability to more contractors as a dependable part of how projects get built.”

“This funding allows us to expand deployments, strengthen the field operations behind every machine, and work with more partners as they integrate intelligent systems into everyday work,” he added. “The opportunity is to help the industry’s experienced crews safely take on more projects, deliver with greater consistency, and quickly deliver more of the infrastructure this country needs.”

Sofman told The Robot Report, “New customer demand is very high. We’re responsibly growing into the demand, bringing on new customers we can serve alongside our longtime design partners. We’re scaling across the board, from operations to hardware to supply chain operations, to keep pace with the needs of our customers.”

Bedrock Robotics adds leadership

In the midst of securing new funding, the company also added two new individuals to the management team.

Amy Jones Satrom joins the leadership team as vice president of operations. She brings operations experience from Amazon, Nuro, and Uber to lead the company in the next phase of scaling to meet demand.

“Amy is instrumental in strengthening our operations and building the systems and support that make successful deployments repeatable,” according to Sofman. “She’s still early in her tenure, but her leadership will be central to growing our deployment and production teams and preparing them to support customers across the country.

“Ajay Gummalla, a co-founder and VP of engineering, is also intimately involved on the hardware side of things, adding resilience to our supply chain so we’re ready to build the hardware we need to meet customer demand,” he explained.

Lando Juarez has joined Bedrock Robotics in the role of general counsel. He was formerly head of legal for Uber’s Autonomous Mobility & Delivery business, overseeing commercial partnerships and regulatory pathways.

Submit your innovation now!

Looking to the future of construction

When asked bout how the company is planning to grow, Sofman responded, “Short term, our growth market remains construction. It is a massive market — 4% to 5% of U.S. GDP — so we’re thinking about expanding use cases. Haydon will test our excavators for autonomous trench work.”

“We’re also thinking about automating larger machine models — Haydon and others will explore bulldozers, ADTs, and wheel loaders as possible heavy machines to automate next,” he said. “Long term: We’re looking at the other industries, like mining and agriculture, that are 1) also dealing with labor constraints and 2) use the same kinds of heavy machines GCs do.”

“For 2027, we are relentlessly focused on getting more Bedrock-equipped machines on more job sites around the country,” Sofman continued. “It was just a few months ago that we first launched fully autonomous excavators on live, commercial job sites, just two years after Bedrock came out of stealth. 2027 is about doubling down on that progress, getting to triple-digit machines working autonomously across the country.”

When asked about the installed base and economic opportunity for Bedrock Robotics’ systems, Sofman was more reserved.

“It’s a bit early to give concrete numbers,” said Sofman, “However, given the labor constraints on general contractors, the math pencils out: Imagine a job that can be completed two months faster because autonomous machines are running around the clock, seven days a week.”

“The developer paying 9% interest on a $400 million loan would save $6 million on that project they can invest into future projects,” he observed. “In turn, construction crews and all the downstream trades, like plumbing and electrical, would see an increasing volume of steady work because there are more projects that can be funded.”

Some data on labor constraints that have opened the market for Bedrock:

  • Twenty percent of construction workers are over the age of 55, and estimates suggest that more than 40% of the construction workers will retire in the next five years.

  • Large projects already run an average of 20% over schedule and 80% over budget.

  • In construction specifically, 87% of firms report openings for hourly craft positions, and 88% say the roles are as hard or harder to fill than a year ago.

OnLogic will keep its Vermont headquarters, as well as its global offices, as part of OMRON. Source: OnLogic

As manufacturers increasingly use data and AI at the edge, they need reliable computing that works alongside real-time automation and control. OMRON Corp. this month said it has agreed to acquire 100% of OnLogic this week, worth $675 million, to combine its proven automation with OnLogic’s industrial computing expertise.

“This acquisition is an important step in advancing our SF2030 vision and our evolution toward GEMBA DX,” stated Junta Tsujinaga, president and CEO of OMRON. “North America is a key growth market for OMRON, and this investment strengthens our foundation there while building the capabilities our customers will increasingly need.”

“OnLogic’s industrial computing expertise, flexibility and strong customer relationships complement our strengths in automation and control,” he added. “Together, we see an opportunity to create new value for customers as manufacturing becomes more connected, data-driven and intelligent.”

Founded in 1933, OMRON Automation creates, sells, and services fully integrated automation solutions that include sensing, control, safety, vision, and motion. The Kyoto, Japan-based company said its 30,000 employees creatively help businesses solve problems in more than 110 countries. Its Americas office is in Hoffman Estates, Ill.

Submit your innovation now!

OnLogic to continue computing brand

Founded in 2003, OnLogic designs and makes configurable, solution-focused, AI-capable computers engineered for reliability at the Internet of Things (IoT) edge. The South Burlington, Vt.-based company said it has helped more than 70,000 customers worldwide with their complex computing challenges with systems that are built to order, delivered in days, and designed to last.

OnLogic noted that its systems operate in the world’s harshest environments across industries. It said joining OMRON will provide industrial automation expertise and access to new markets.

“We built OnLogic to help engineers and innovators solve tough technology challenges by making custom, rugged hardware easy to configure, build, and deploy,” said Sean Larkin, CEO of OnLogic. “Joining OMRON provides the global scale, supply chain depth, and capital resources to accelerate our product roadmaps while preserving our culture, direct sales approach, and operations around the world. Together, we are giving our customers the tools they need to deploy physical AI with confidence.”

Following the acquisition, OnLogic will continue to operate as an independent business within the OMRON Group. It will keep its offices in the U.S., the Netherlands, Germany, Taiwan, and Malaysia, as well as its brand identity and direct sales model.

OnLogic’s management team, led by Larkin, will remain in place to drive day-to-day operations and strategic growth.

OMRON sees opportunities for manufacturers

The companies said they will help customers address increasingly complex applications that require greater processing power, connectivity, and intelligence at the edge. OMRON has experience in control, robotics, and safety.

OnLogic brings configurable computing platforms designed for demanding applications and environments, as well as its flexible build-to-order model and customer reach across manufacturing and other markets.

The companies said they expect to more closely connect machine data, edge computing, and AI with real-time automation and control. Over time, the combination is expected to create systems that help turn data, insights, and AI into faster, more informed actions to optimize manufacturing.

OMRON added that the acquisition is an investment in its Industrial Automation Business and strengthens the company’s position in the Americas and Europe. OnLogic has relationships with customers across both traditional automation markets and industries where OMRON sees additional opportunities for growth.

In addition, OMRON said it remains committed to its established channel strategy and to continuing to invest in and support the partners that help it serve customers and grow in the market. The companies said they expect the acquisition to close in or around January 2027, subject to regulatory approval.

Agility and GXO have been collaborating since 2023. Source: Agility Robotics

Agility Robotics and GXO Logistics today said they are expanding their partnership to deploy Agility’s Digit humanoid robot in GXO sites in North Carolina and Tennessee.

“GXO was the first customer to put Digit to work in live operations under a commercial agreement, and expanding to additional sites is the clearest signal that the value is real,” stated Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility. “Customers are moving beyond asking whether humanoid robots can work to deciding where they can scale them. Years of experience performing real work in GXO’s operations have shaped how we build, deploy and support Digit, and we’re focused on disciplined execution as we grow this partnership.”

Founded in 2015, Agility Robotics said it has more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation working with industry safety standards. The Salem, Ore.-based company recently got U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission approval for its planned merger with special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Churchill Capital Corp. XI as it prepares to go public.

In 2024, Digit earned Agility the inaugural RBR50 Robot of the Year award for being one of the first humanoids to enter commercial trials. It received 2026 honors for moving more than 100,000 totes for GXO last year. This month, the company chose Nyobolt for fast charging, expanded its partnership with NVIDIA, and said it plans to deploy Digit at an AGCO factory for agricultural equipment in 2027.

Generative Bionics this week announced plans to build a proprietary, multi-site “Physical AI Data Factory” in Italy. The company said the new 5,000-sq.-m (53,819.5-sq.-ft.) hub will help move humanoid robotics from laboratory demonstrations to reliable industrial deployment.

In addition, Generative Bionics said it hopes to advance European humanoid sovereignty, ensuring that the data, models, and know-how behind Europe’s industrial humanoids are generated, trained and validated on the continent.

“The value that Europe has right now is within its industry, and we have to extract physical AI data in order to train our own models,” Daniele Pucci, the CEO of Generative Bionics, told The Robot Report. “This is a competitive advantage that Europe right now has, because of the automation that we have been putting in place over the last 40 years.”

Generative Bionics said the new facility will be operational by the fourth quarter of 2027. The Genoa, Italy-based company plans to eventually open a second facility elsewhere in Europe and a third serving global markets. Together, the three facilities will reproduce real industrial environments, generate high-fidelity physical data, and connect that data with large-scale simulation.

Building on their strategic technology collaboration, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. will be Generative Bionics’ AI infrastructure partner, and the Physical AI Data Factory network will be powered by AMD Helios. Its rack-scale architecture will provide the compute foundation to process physical and synthetic data, train physical AI models, and run thousands of digital-twin scenario variations in parallel.

Data Factory to test GENE.01 in a range of industries

The Physical AI Data Factory will connect real-world robot operations, simulation and AI development in a continuous real-to-sim-to-real cycle, said Generative Bionics. The company said this will allow it to configure and validate its GENE.01 humanoid robot for specific industrial environments before customer deployment, then feed data from deployed fleets into future training cycles.

Industrial humanoids must learn from the conditions they will encounter at work, noted the Generative Bionics. This requires data that captures contact, force, motion, proximity, temperature, task constraints, and human interaction in realistic operating settings. For GENE.01, the dataset will include vision and motion data as well as signals captured through its full-body multimodal skin.

“A robot is not only vision and is not only language,” said Pucci. “It is position, velocity, acceleration, temperature, and contact forces, so there is a large variety of data that you have to take into account.”

The Data Factory will reproduce environments selected with industrial partners and allow fleets of GENE.01 robots to perform tasks continuously in real-world conditions. These operations will generate high-fidelity physical data for training world action models (WAM) and validating the complete robot system, including perception, control, safety behavior, and task execution, before deployment at customer sites.

Each physical environment and robot configuration will also be recreated as a digital twin. The same tasks can then be repeated across thousands of variations in layout, objects, materials, operating conditions, and failure modes that would be impractical to reproduce physically. Models trained and tested in simulation will be deployed back to the robots for validation, while data from physical operations will feed the next training cycle.

Generative Bionics wants to help find robot ‘ChatGPT moment’

Large language models (LLMs) learn from vast amounts of information available online, noted Generative Bionics. Humanoid robots have no comparable source of data on how to act in the physical world.

The Physical AI Data Factory will create such a source by collecting data as GENE.01 performs industrial tasks and expanding those experiences through digital-twins running on AMD compute.

“We have the ambition of being the European champion in physical AI, and even robotics, designed to scale globally,” said Pucci. “That’s our clear positioning, and for this, we are taking a close look at the supply chain that can supply our future manufacturing.”

“Manufacturing here is divided into three levels: the manufacturing of data, the manufacturing of robots, and the manufacturing of models,” she continued. Pucci said if Europe wants to achieve sovereignty in this area, it needs to invest in all three.

Right now, humanoid robots from China have been garnering a lot of attention with flashy demos and large funding rounds. But, Pucci, notes that this doesn’t mean the country is necessarily ahead of Europe.

“I want to be crystal clear about this. Many of the Chinese robots that are out there are simply not certified to enter industrial settings,” Pucci said. “The narrative that the Chinese solved as the issues is very far from reality.”

“Right now, we believe that many of the existing solutions are basically for entertainment, and this is a market segment that we respect,” she added. “But, Generative Bionics is taking the issue of safety and certification very seriously because we want to go B2B first.”

Generative Bionics claimed that a few things separate its platform from the average humanoid robot. To start, GENE.01 features full-body tactile sensing.

“This is really scalable at the manufacturing level, because you have a common platform, and then you can customize at the end the so-called end of lines at these three levels,” she continued. “This is basically the same approach that you have in automotive.”

Generative Bionics is building on more than 20 years of research, development, and prototyping of humanoids at the Italian Institute of Technology (IIT). The company spun out of IIT in 2024, and IIT has granted it exclusive licenses to key technologies.

Robotics Summit & Expo West is organized around the questions that define the post-prototype stage of a robotics company:

Deployment at scale: What changes when a robot moves from a controlled pilot to multiple live sites, including integration, fleet management, remote monitoring, and autonomous operations in increasingly unstructured environments.

Go-to-market and commercial strategy: How robotics companies are responding to market demand and structuring pricing, sales, and channel strategies for products that combine hardware, software, and services.

Field data and product decisions: How real-world performance data flows back into product iteration and AI model evolution. Ongoing service and support, whether directly or through partners, is also key to demonstrating a return on investment.

Investment and growth: How investors evaluate robotics companies, and how founding teams can build businesses that last.

Avenda Health said it designed Surgery Mode to enhance how surgeons use 3D AI mapping during non-robotic and robotic surgeries, alongside new tools to simplify patient case management and physician workflows.

The launch builds on peer-reviewed research predicting that Unfold AI could cut positive surgical margins in half, substantially reducing cancer recurrence. In the study, the system outperformed MRI and other modalities in assessing whether cancer had spread beyond the prostate, assisting surgeons in making nerve-sparing decisions.

In Surgery Mode, physicians can now access enlarged 3D views for clearer visualization, adjust the cancer estimation map to match the camera angle on the surgical console, review underlying MRI slices during the procedure, and access capsule risk scores from within a dedicated surgical view.

Avenda Health claimed that Unfold AI is the only platform implementing multimodal AI to analyze a patient’s MRI, biopsy, pathology, and PSA together. It produces a personalized 3D map of the cancer’s extent to provide surgeons with more precise visualization of tumor boundaries.

The suite of improved workflow tools also gives physicians and staff greater visibility into the status of each patient case.

At 12:15 p.m., Bhavana Chandrashekhar, the senior manager of applied science at Amazon Robotics, and Joyce Sidopoulos, co-founder and chief of operations at MassRobotics, will start the Women in Robotics Luncheon. This ticketed event will include a fireside chat between the two tech leaders. It presents an opportunity for women in the industry to form connections, deepen relationships, and champion increased female representation in robotics leadership.

RoboBusiness 2026 beakout sessions will resume in the afternoon. Sessions starting at 1:15 p.m. include:

  • From Models to Machines: Building the Open Infrastructure for Physical AI: Nagesh Puppala, the general manager of physical AI and robotics at Intel, will explore the infrastructure required to move physical AI from prototype to production in real-world robotics systems. The talk will be in Room 209/210.
  • State of Robotics Investments: Sanjay Aggarwal, a venture partner at F-Prime Capital, and Betsy Mulé, a principal at F-Prime, will unveil the firm’s annual “State of Robotics Investments” report, highlighting the latest funding trends, emerging technology categories, and the sectors attracting the most investor interest. The session will take place in Room 207.
  • Closing the Capability Gap: A Leadership Framework for Scaling Field Robotics: Kenrick Tjandra, the robot deployment lead of Raise Robotics, will provide attendees with a decision rule for allocating engineering capacity, a vocabulary for two hidden failure modes, and the pre-mobilization gates that keep field programs from stalling. He will explain the discipline that separates a demo from a system that scales. His talk will be in Room 206.
  • Beyond the Pilot: What It Takes to Put Humanoids to Work in Manufacturing: Dr. Weiwei Chen, the founder and CEO of EmbodyX, will share what the company has learned deploying humanoids in real manufacturing environments. This RoboBusiness 2026 session will be in Room 203.
  • How Robotics and Physical AI are Transforming Modular Data Center Construction: Ali Raja, the vice president of data centers at ABB Robotics, will explore how robotics, prefabrication and modular construction can work together to streamline delivery, reduce pressure on scarce labor and scale data center capacity. The talk will be in Room 204.

Talks starting at 2:15 p.m. include:

  • Physical AI Doesn’t Have a Data Problem; It Has a Deployment Problem: Rudy Cohen, the co-founder and CEO of Inbolt, will reframe where physical AI actually pays off. Cohen said this happens not in bigger models, but in closing the loop at servo frequency and collapsing the months of fixtures, wiring, and retuning that make every deployment a six-figure project. This will take place in Room 209/210.
  • The Economics of Robotics: Is This Business Viable? Jack Pearson, an investment principal at RoboStrategy, will offer a set of mental models for judging whether a robotics business can create real value and capture it in a way that lasts. The session will be in Room 207.
  • Lessons Learned Building Reliable Outdoor Robots: This panel will feature insights from Ben Waters, co-founder and CEO of WiBotic; Vibhor Sood, co-founder and VP of engineering at Burro; Derek Chase, the vice president of robotics and AI at Nextpower; and Ben Choster, the founder of Catalyze Robotics. The panel will demonstrate how engineering decisions impact reliability, uptime, operational efficiency, and total cost of ownership. It will take place in Room 206.
  • A Crash Course in Force & Torque Sensing for Humanoids: Robert Brooks, the founder and CEO of ForceN, will summarize learnings from working with many of world’s top humanoid companies over the past three years. His talk will be in Room 203.
  • Functional Safety for Humanoid Actuators: Jordan Schaeffer, the manager of business development at Novanta, will explore how safe motion, torque control, fault detection, and actuator-level safety functions can help reduce risk while maintaining performance. The talk will take place in Room 204.

RoboBusiness 2026 talks starting at 3:30 p.m. include:

  • How Agentic Coding Empowers Lean Teams to Build Faster: Anthony Jules, the co-founder and chief innovation officer at Robust AI, will explore how AI agents are transforming the robotics development lifecycle right from the initial design phase. The talk will be in Room 209/210.
  • The RaaS Playbook: Pricing, Service & Scale: This panel will include insights from Rick Faulk, the CEO of Locus Robotics; Bill Booth, who leads technology sales, marketing, and business development at Roboworx; and Alex Linde, the chief product officer at Aescape. The speakers will provide attendees with practical strategies for building sustainable RaaS offerings that deliver value for both robotics providers and their customers. The panel will take place in Room 207.
  • Designing Dexterous Learning Robots for Outdoor Labor: Brent Shedd, the founder and CEO of AgRobotics, will deliver a practitioner-level framework: What’s working, what’s hard, and what a realistic path to commercial deployment actually looks like. The talk will be in Room 206.
  • Can Humanoids be Safe? Benjamin Twombly, the founder and CEO of Critical Systems Analysis, will share insights into both the continuity and the evolution of safety thinking as it adapts to intelligent, human-like machines operating in dynamic, real-world contexts. His session will take place in Room 203.
  • What AI-Defined Automation Looks Like in Production: François Giguére, the chief technology officer at Vention, will give attendees a framework for evaluating AI-defined automation in their own operations. The talk will be in Room 204.

Engineering Theater talks

On the show floor, we’ll be running talks in the Engineering Theater throughout the day. The talks include:

  • Sensor Solutions for Humanoids: Tools to Build the Future: Uma Krishnamoorthy, the senior director of core technology at InvenSense, will explore sensing solutions enabling today’s humanoid innovations. Her talk will start at 11:00 a.m.
  • The Robot Out of the Cage. Advanced Functional Safety for Humanoids: Jan Kaiser, the head of marketing at Synapticon, will discuss how certifiable safety architecture will lay a path towards real-world deployments for humanoids. The talk will start at 11:45 a.m.
  • From First Flash to Field Repair: Servicing Robots From a Tablet: Reed Giovannetti, co-founder and CEO of DeviceNexus, will work through the engineering questions behind keeping robots running, on the bench and in the field. This session will begin at 12:30 p.m.
  • Simulation Said Go. The Binary Said No: Keeping Robots Inside Their Requirements in the AI Era: Stojan Gancev, the VP of R&D at Aurora Labs, will discuss the importance of reasoning straight from the architecture, from the compiled binary sitting on the target processor, rather than trusting review and simulation to catch what they structurally cannot see. It will start at 2:00 p.m.
  • Shared Spaces: Navigating Challenges for Indoor Robots: This RoboBusiness 2026 panel session will include insights from Aaron Edsinger, co-founder and CEO of Hello Robot, and Matt Anderson, co-founder and CEO of A&K Robotics. The two will discuss how solving navigation challenges will be critical to achieving broad consumer acceptance and large-scale deployment. It will start at 3:30 p.m.

]]> London/NY-based Nevis, an AI OS for wealth management, today announced its €62 million ($70 million) Series B in order to expand agent capabilities, deepen integrations across the custodian and WealthTech ecosystem, and grow its product and GTM teams.

The round was led by EQT Ventures, bringing total funding to €98 million ($110 million) in two years since founding. New strategic investors include The Charles Schwab Corporation, and QuantumLight, the fund of Revolut founder and CEO Nik Storonsky. All existing investors, including Sequoia Capital, ICONIQ and Ribbit Capital, have also expanded their commitments in this new round.

“Our customers measure Nevis in business results: more client calls, hours back every week, and accounts opened every day. Nevis agents finish the work, so every advisor can give every client the white-glove attention of a full-service team,” says Mark Swan, CEO and co-founder of Nevis. “We’re proud to have investors who see this industry from the inside backing our work to make AI agents core infrastructure for advisory firms.”

Elsewhere in Europe, 2026 funding for software serving wealth managers and financial advisers has included Copenhagen-based Performativ’s €11.96 million Series A, TODAY’s €2.8 million Seed round, and Zurich-based Aisot Technologies’ €2.13 million Seed extension.

In the UK, London’s WealthAi raised €837k for its AI-powered wealth management platform, while Glasgow-based Afternoon Finance secured €57k for financial-adviser automation software. Broader related British announcements include Fifth Dimension’s €22 million Series A and Vennre’s €8 million funding.

Together, these rounds represent approximately €47.8 million in 2026 funding, excluding Nevis’ Series B.

“Mark, Philipp and Ivan have built an exceptional AI platform at a time when wealth management faces a growing capacity gap, with advisors retiring as demand for advice rises. Nevis is helping firms serve more clients and scale efficiently. We’re excited to bring EQT’s network across wealth management and financial services to support their growth and ambition to become the foundational AI platform for the industry,” adds Carolina Brochado, Partner and Head of EQT Ventures.

Founded in 2024 by Mark Swan (CEO), Philipp Burda (Chief Product Officer), and Ivan Chalov (COO); Nevis builds AI products to automate the administrative work of financial advisors. Nevis’ customers represent more than €625 billion ($700 billion) in client assets.

By bringing CRM, meeting intelligence, financial planning, and custodial workflows together in a single AI platform, Nevis agents handle operational work end-to-end and have completed more than 100,000 operational tasks.

Across customer deployments, Nevis says they are enabling financial advisors to:

  • Reclaim up to 10 hours every week
  • Increase prospect meetings by 30%
  • Generate personalised financial plans and prospect proposals in minutes
  • Accelerate account opening from weeks to days

“We’ve built an AI ecosystem that gives advisors greater choice and access to capabilities that can help them run and grow their firms,” says Jon Beatty, head of Schwab Advisor Services. “Our investment in and partnership with Nevis expands that ecosystem, helping advisors harness AI to operate more efficiently, increase their capacity and ultimately serve more investors.”

Today’s funding coincides with a year of rapid growth, having reportedly grown revenue more than 25x. Customers include Focus Financial Partners, IEQ Capital and United Capital.

The post The 2026 PR playbook for startups: execution appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Part one was about strategy: the “why” behind PR, which stakeholders to chase, how to move them, and which media channels to pursue. You have the map, but now you need to understand the territory and how to move effectively inside of it.

Three practical considerations remain before you are ready to pitch: what actually earns a journalist’s attention, which activities are worth the effort, and how to conduct yourself effectively and ethically.

Newsworthiness

So what makes it to the media? Can you pitch anything you want? Not really. To determine what gets covered and what doesn’t, it helps to understand the concept of newsworthiness. If something is newsworthy, it is important and interesting enough to be covered in the media (whether it’s a news announcement or not).

The “gatekeepers” mentioned in the last piece all have their own perceptions of what is and isn’t newsworthy. Newsworthiness varies by outlet, by person, and changes with time. We can break it down into five main components.

Timeliness comes first and can be determined in two ways: short-term and long-term. Short-term timeliness is controllable, as the source decides when newsworthy information, such as funding announcements, is released to the media and typically covered that same day. Long-term timeliness, however, depends on external developments beyond the source’s control, such as breaking news, regulatory changes, or cultural trends that align with the current zeitgeist.

The second factor is impact. And when we say impact, we mean scale. Some stories make it based on sheer size because they involve staggering revenue, eye-watering funding rounds, or skyrocketing headcount. Bigger numbers make bigger stories, which explains why funding rounds remain such reliable triggers. They arrive with a figure and a set of backers that together signal validation. To be clear, a non-funding-related action that has an outsize effect on the industry, society or a human life, is equally newsworthy. A case study of new technology that saved a person’s life, which would have not been otherwise possible, is also a good example of impact.

Geography matters more than founders expect. A national desk may wave aside what a local or regional outlet would treat as a genuine event, and trade titles care about their own patch above all else. Starting close to home is usually the easiest way in, and it is the lever most startups overlook. Wanting US or UK hits as a small startup in mainland Europe is usually wishful thinking, but European startup outlets may have better openings.

Name recognition goes a long way. A well-known investor, a notable advisor, or a marquee client can elevate an entire story by lending credibility. A journalist who would pass on an unknown startup will often look twice when a familiar name is involved. “Celebrity” counts, especially if you have a real celebrity, like when the legal AI platform Legora hired the aptly-named Jude Law as a spokesperson.

Conflict is the most volatile of the five factors. Newsrooms are drawn to tension and disagreement, but picking fights can backfire on young companies trying to build goodwill. There are exceptions, mostly in the form of a clear, defensible stance on the trajectory of your industry. (Mudslinging at competitors is not something wise for early stage startups to do.) Even so, this is a rare exception, not a strategy.

Before pitching anything, look hard at your own company, technology, product and people, and be objective about genuine newsworthiness versus merely interesting to you. Study your target channels, and what they cover. What do they find newsworthy? That will show you what is newsworthy, to whom, and where.

Activity tracks

Across those channels, think in terms of sustained activities rather than one-off hits. Three tracks are worth knowing.

News is the obvious and easiest one. For an early startup, a funding announcement is usually the most valuable of all. It carries a number and a set of named backers, which together read as validation you cannot otherwise claim alone. Milestones such as a new product launch, a marquee customer, a new market, a hire senior enough to signal intent work similarly, but may be newsworthy only in trade and smaller media. For news, journalists tend to appreciate a well-written, factual press release. Don’t believe those that say the press release is dead!

Thought leadership is the second track, and the most misunderstood. It’s not shameless self-promotion, just like PR isn’t. It’s a contribution to the industry and community by sharing a point of view, insight or constructive criticism about your field. It’s your contribution to a larger conversation. In PR, the value of that contribution needs to be substantial enough to warrant a third-party media platform, which in turn lends you a higher level of credibility. Thought leadership comes in many forms, but op-eds, podcasts and speaking slots are the most common. 

Profiling is the third. It can take the form of Q&As, features and company or executive profiles that give a face and human identity to a business. Sometimes labelled “slots” or “series“, these are out there for the taking once you have traction, so understand which outlets and journalists do them, what truly interests them, and pitch them.

Not everyone has frequent newsworthy items or time for thought leadership. But ideally, you’ll have a good enough mix. Once you’re solid in your PR journey, more activity tracks become available, but that’s for another time.

Keep it human

A last word, because this is where the whole thing can come undone. Everything rests on real people trusting real people. The temptation to automate the human away is strong and growing. A PR agency was recently caught pitching journalists using a roster of fake, AI-generated PR pros, all without telling clients. Journalists notice, and they do not forgive it.

A similar logic applies to a number of other lazy shortcuts: blasting emails without checking relevance, fully AI-written pitches, etc. It wastes journalists’ time and weakens your credibility, and it is the quickest way to undo months of careful work. Use AI the way good journalists do. Follow them and see what they think about AI, you’ll find they appreciate it for research, analysing notes and internal documents and a number of other secondary tasks. This is a very fluid area, so stay up to date.

Your PR methodology

PR is not rocket science, but few take the time to learn it. This article aims to be less a set of tactics than a practical framework to help founders think about PR without overcomplicating it.

A reputation doesn’t rest on one headline but many trusted sources over time that tell a consistent story about who you are. Build that, and the big title you always wanted might eventually come to you. But never mistake the foundation for the cherry on top.

]]> EU Inc. survives Council negotiations, but are Europe’s founders getting what they asked for? https://www.eu-startups.com/2026/10/eu-inc-survives-council-negotiations-but-are-europes-startup-founders-getting-what-they-asked-for/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 12:25:11 +0000 https://www.eu-startups.com/?p=372676 On Friday, 23 October 2026, the Council of the European Union adopted its negotiating position on the proposed 28th corporate regime (EU Inc.), retaining the ambition of allowing companies to incorporate online within 48 hours for no more than €100 and operate across the EU single market. The agreement comes just over a week after […]

The post EU Inc. survives Council negotiations, but are Europe’s founders getting what they asked for? appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> On Friday, 23 October 2026, the Council of the European Union adopted its negotiating position on the proposed 28th corporate regime (EU Inc.), retaining the ambition of allowing companies to incorporate online within 48 hours for no more than €100 and operate across the EU single market.

The agreement comes just over a week after the EU–INC campaign, backed by more than 26,000 founders, investors and startup operators from across Europe, warned that the legislation was being stripped of its most important provisions.

But the questions remains: Are Europe’s founders getting what they asked for? Or the watered down version?

A win, with strings attached

One of the most significant developments is the survival of the proposed European Employee Stock Option Plan (EU-ESO), a mechanism designed to help startups attract and retain talent.

In its earlier warning, the EU–INC campaign argued that removing harmonised stock-option rules would undermine one of the framework’s central advantages. Startups often depend on equity incentives to compete for employees against larger companies offering higher salaries.

The Council has now retained the scheme, including provisions intended to defer taxation until shares are sold, rather than when options are granted, vested or exercised.

However, eligibility has been tightened. The Council’s position restricts the relevant tax provisions to companies with fewer than 750 employees and annual turnover not exceeding €150 million, compared with an earlier compromise proposing thresholds of 1,000 employees and €450 million.

Dr. Peter Möllmann, founding partner of German law firm PXR, shares with EU-Startups: “The Council has preserved the original idea of EU Inc. as an optional, digital and Europe-wide regime. But the more restrictions and national safeguards are added, the greater the risk that Europe creates a politically acceptable framework that founders and investors will simply not use.”

The missing pieces

Other concerns raised by the startup community appear less resolved.

The Council’s full negotiating mandate confirms that plans for a central European company register have been removed, alongside the requirement for real-time tracking of registrations.

Although digital registration and a simplified digital share register remain part of the framework, these are not equivalent to a single centralised European company register.

For founders and investors, the distinction matters. A shared registration infrastructure could have helped simplify due diligence, company verification and cross-border financing. Without it, businesses may still need to navigate different national administrative systems.

The Council has also removed the dedicated insolvency chapter from the Commission’s original proposal. This means EU Inc. companies would continue to face applicable national insolvency rules rather than benefiting from the proposed simplified European procedures.

Another unresolved issue concerns freedom of incorporation. The Council maintains the optional nature of EU Inc., allowing companies to choose the new framework instead of existing national corporate forms. However, the structure will still operate within national legal systems, which will govern matters not harmonised by the regulation.

This leaves open the concern that the regime could develop into 27 national variations rather than becoming the recognisable, predictable European standard sought by its supporters.

Despite this, Micheál Martin, Taoiseach of Ireland (the country currently holding the presidency of the Council of the European Union), was positive in his comment shared to the press.

“I warmly welcome the agreement on ‘EU Inc.’ reached in the Council today. As Presidency, Ireland has placed strong emphasis on improving Europe’s competitiveness. This is a measure that will make a real and practical difference to startups and SMEs looking to scale up across the EU. It will be easier to establish, easier to attract and retain talented staff, easier to take advantage of the Single Market, one of Europe’s greatest strengths.”

Workers’ rights in focus

The Council’s position also attempts to address concerns raised by European trade unions, which have warned that the new structure could allow businesses to take advantage of differences between national employment and corporate governance rules.

Under the negotiating mandate, EU Inc. companies would generally remain subject to the employee participation rules of the member state where they have their registered office.

However, the Council has introduced an optional mechanism allowing member states to address situations where a company incorporated elsewhere exceeds employee participation thresholds in their territory.

The agreement also strengthens safeguards against abuse, permitting national authorities to delay or refuse registration on grounds relating to money laundering, terrorist financing or other criminal activity.

These provisions are aimed at calming concerns about regulatory arbitrage and employee representation – although the optional nature of the participation mechanism leaves questions about consistency across the EU.

This introduces a potential trade-off. Additional national checks may offer stronger protections, but could make implementation more complex and weaken the simplicity that entrepreneurs originally sought.

Taxation remains another limitation. Beyond the specific provisions for employee stock options, EU Inc. does not create a unified European tax regime. Companies would continue to comply with applicable national corporate tax, VAT and employment obligations.

What’s next?

Friday’s agreement represents a political milestone, but EU Inc. has not yet become law. The Council has adopted its negotiating mandate, establishing the position that member states will defend in discussions with the European Parliament.

The Parliament still has to establish its own position on the proposal, which could seek to restore, add or remove elements of EU Inc. As of 26 October 2026, the status of the legislative file remains at “Awaiting committee decision“.

Once Parliament agrees its negotiating position, representatives of the Parliament, Council and Commission can begin interinstitutional negotiations, commonly known as trilogues, to establish a final legislative text.

The Council is also proposing a 21-month implementation period. Meaning even if EU institutions reach an agreement before the end of 2026, companies would not immediately be able to register under the new regime.

But there are reasons for cautious optimism. The proposed framework remains alive, its principal incorporation commitments have survived and the employee stock-option scheme has been retained, albeit in a more restricted form.

The next stage will determine whether the European institutions can reconcile the competing demands for simplicity, investor confidence and regulatory protection without compromising the framework’s usefulness.

Editor’s Note: EU–INC is an independent, founder-led advocacy campaign pushing for a common European startup standard, while EU Inc. is the European Commission’s proposed corporate legal framework, introduced on 18 March 2026. The campaign helped build momentum behind the reform but does not control the legislative process.

]]> Z_One Fund, the Italian venture capital fund managed by Eureka! Venture has announced the first close at more than €35 million, with a total fundraising target of €60 million.

The fund’s investor base includes some of Italy’s most prominent institutional investors. CDP Venture Capital SGR has committed capital through its newly launched Fondo Acceleratori 2. Other investors include Euronext Milan-listed Zest, Lazio Innova through a parallel fund focused on the Lazio region, Fondazione Compagnia di San Paolo, and a number of private investors.

“The development of an increasingly mature innovation ecosystem comes from the ability to value specialised operators capable of supporting startups from the earliest stages of growth. It is with this vision that we chose to invest in Z_One Fund, the first investment of the Fondo Acceleratori 2, the cornerstone of our new acceleration strategy, designed to leverage the skills of specialised managers and operators, while maintaining the Rete Nazionale Acceleratori’s ability to combine investment with operational and mentorship support to help companies with go-to-market and the validation of their business model,” said Stefano Molino, Head of the Fondo Acceleratori at CDP Venture Capital.

Luigi Capello, a pioneer of the Italian innovation ecosystem, leads the fund alongside partner Giulio Montoli and junior partner Giulia Fazzini. Montoli has built his career in acceleration and pre-Seed investing, including leading the management of one of the country’s largest startup portfolios, while Fazzini is one of the youngest women to hold a partner-level role at an Italian VC firm.

Collectively, they bring experience of over 340 investments, more than 25 exits, and over €80 million under management, with notable deals including FitPrime, Robot.com, JetHR, Vikey and 2Hire. The fund targets pre-Seed and Seed stage startups across two focus areas: AI Applications and UrbanTech and Smart Cities.

In AI Applications, the fund will back startups embedding artificial intelligence into corporate and public administration workflows, covering verticals from financial services and retail to digital security and the development of new AI models. In UrbanTech and Smart Cities, the fund is focusing on technologies transforming cities, including smart buildings, electric mobility, water and waste management, and the regeneration of public spaces.

“Italian venture capital needs a financial supply chain to help high-potential startups grow. This requires institutional capital willing to invest from the very beginning and the ability to support founders in developing their business. With Z_One Fund we put to use the experience gained over years of investing and acceleration,” said Capello, Partner at Z_One Fund.

He added, “We want to give more teams the opportunity to test themselves against the market and to progressively concentrate resources on the companies that show the greatest potential, in segments that open up important opportunities for a new generation of tech companies. Our ambition is to help them be born in Italy with a European outlook.”

Z_One Fund is managed by Eureka! Venture, an independent Milan-based asset management company founded in 2019 and supervised by the Bank of Italy and Consob. The firm is focused exclusively on DeepTech investments and recently launched Eureka! Fund II – Deep Tech Lazio, a €20 million early-stage fund. To date, the firm has raised over €190 million across a multi-strategy platform spanning technology transfer, software, DeepTech, AI, UrbanTech, and SME-focused vehicles.

The Z-One Fund aims to be the first institutional cheque to startups with initial tickets up to €250k, with selective follow-on investments of up to €1 million. The fund is also part of CDP Venture Capital’s Rete Nazionale Acceleratori, which means portfolio companies will receive not just funding but also access to a structured acceleration programme delivered in partnership with Zest.

“With Z_One Fund we take a further step in Eureka!’s growth path as a multi-strategy platform dedicated to alternative investments. We believe venture capital needs increasingly specialised and vertical models, capable of combining entrepreneurial talent, capital, expertise and operational support,” said Stefano Peroncini, CEO of Eureka! Venture SGR, manager of Z_One Fund.

Alongside the main vehicle sits Z_One Fund Lazio, a parallel fund created through the Lazio Venture 2 initiative under the PR FESR 2021-2027 programme and managed by Lazio Innova.

The parallel fund applies the same investment strategy as Z_One Fund while directing capital specifically toward startups connected to the Lazio region, aiming to strengthen the availability of pre-Seed and Seed financing locally and bridge innovation with regional universities and industry.

]]> In response to recent reports of Russian advancement in drone and missile production, German military AI startup Helsing has unveiled Contra; an AI-controlled autonomous air defence system against scaled drone and missile attacks.

The company also introduced two advanced interceptor missiles, AD-1 Inferno and AD-2 Ambush, designed to outmatch and outrun even the fastest jet-powered drone and cruise missile threats.

Niklas Köhler, co-founder and President of Helsing, says: “Contra ends the air defence dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometres high–affordable and at industrial scale.”

This comes during a competitive landscape for European DefenceTech spending and activity.

EU-Startups has reported approximately €511 million in financing across European startups developing interceptor systems, counter-drone technologies and related autonomous capabilities in 2026.

Among the closest comparisons, UK-based Cambridge Aerospace secured €173.1 million in April and a further €259.7 million in August to scale affordable air-defence interceptors, while Estonia’s Frankenburg Technologies raised €30 million to expand missile manufacturing.

In Germany, Hannover-based INLEAP Photonics secured €20 million for laser-based drone defence, alongside smaller investments in Denmark’s Shotling (€700k) and Sweden’s Freya Industries (€533k).

Related autonomy investments included €12 million for Norway’s Six Robotics and €15 million for Finland’s Kelluu. Separately, German unmanned-systems developer Quantum Systems raised €1 billion in July. Helsing itself previously secured a €600 million Series D in June 2025, as documented by EU-Startups.

Founded in 2021 in Munich, Helsing is a Military AI company that designs new types of AI-defined and autonomous systems across multiple domains.

According to the company, recent intelligence indicates that Russia has systematically increased its jet-powered drone and cruise missile production, with Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drone output alone rising to 4,000 units per month. At the same time, Russia is constructing numerous additional launch sites for such drones.

This reportedly brings parts of the EU within range of potential Russian attacks.

Contra is designed to counter this threat. Autonomous AI-based operation allows the detection and engagement of hundreds or thousands of drone and missile threats at the same time by fusing sensors and effectors into a single air picture. With Helsing’s Altra C2 platform as the foundation, users allegedly retain full control over decision making and prioritisation.

To effectively engage large numbers of fast aerial targets, Helsing is also developing two missile interceptors with advanced radar seekers:

  • AD-1 Inferno is a jet-powered interceptor capable of aerial loitering, swarming, and repeated re-engagements.
  • AD-2 Ambush is a solid-rocket – motor (SRM) missile for rapid intercepts, reaching Mach 2.5 and a range of 20km+.

Both systems receive mid-course guidance from Contra radar ground stations and feature an advanced onboard radar-seeker for all-weather terminal guidance. Both interceptors are container-launched.

Mass production will take place at Helsing’s Resilience Factories, with unit prices reportedly undercutting those of existing missile interceptors.

While AD-1 and AD-2 form an essential part of the Contra offering, the system is natively set up to integrate third-party hardware, such as other interceptors, cUAV lasers, cUAV guns or net-based systems.

The compant says that Contra reflects their cross-domain approach: using AI and software to draw high capability from affordable, mass-producible hardware. The result is autonomous fire dominance at scale that remains under human control.

The funding came from Springvest, with backing from both new and existing investors, including venture capital firm Maki.vc.

“Volare 01 proves that our technology and production model work at industrial scale. We delivered the factory on schedule and on budget, demonstrating our ability to build production capacity cost-effectively and laying a strong foundation for further growth,” said Jarna Hyvönen, CEO and co-founder of Volare.

Founded in 2021 by Tuure Parviainen, Matti Tähtinen, and Hyvönen as a spin-off from VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, Volare began working on its technology way back in 2014. The company has successfully brought its technology from lab to industrial production, which relies on the Black soldier fly, described by the company as nature’s own bioreactor.

The insect is fed food-industry side streams, and within roughly a week of active growth, converts them into protein and oil. Volare has built a proprietary, highly automated production process that covers the full chain, from rearing larvae to finished ingredients. It says the result is a facility that generates no process wastewater, runs entirely on non-fossil fuel energy, and operates with just four people per shift.

Volare 01, its new 10,000-square-metre plant, targets annual production of up to 5,000 tonnes of insect protein and 2,000 tonnes of insect oil, converting food-industry side streams into high-value ingredients for aquafeed, pet food, and poultry feed markets. Instead of building the factory from scratch, the company built the facility inside a former newspaper printing hall, an approach that reduces construction requirements and costs.

The company says the facility was delivered on schedule and within its €15 million budget. Volare 01 represents a thousandfold expansion from the company’s demonstration plant, yet relies on the same production process that has been commercially validated over four years.

Compared with other insect-based producers, Volare claims its factory requires four to ten times less capital expenditure, around 50% fewer full-time employees, and 30% less energy for end-product processing. Its protein meal delivers over 90% digestibility.

A significant share of Volare 01’s production capacity has already been sold with offtake agreements in place with Skretting, one of the world’s largest aqua feed companies and a leading global chemical company.

Volare says its protein has been commercially used since 2022, featuring in insect-based dog treats developed with Alvar Pet, cat food under Dagsmark’s (Vafo Group brand), and rainbow trout feed through a collaboration with Alltech Fennoaqua.

The €7.1 million in fresh funding will be used to finance a second factory and a broader push across and beyond Europe. With Volare 01 now operational and financing secured for a second facility, the Finnish company is preparing itself for a roadmap that spans multiple plants across Europe, built in partnership with food industry players who generate the side streams it processes.

“Europe needs significantly more locally produced protein, and we have built a model that can deliver it efficiently and competitively. Our next step is to replicate our model from Finland and bring more local, efficient protein production capacity to Europe and beyond,” Hyvönen added.

]]> Sonexos, a Lausanne-based DeepTech company, has raised approximately €5.4 million (CHF 5 million/USD 6.1 million) in new equity financing to take its solid-state noise control from working prototypes to industrial production.

The round was led by Valquest Partners, with participation from Robert Bosch Venture Capital GmbH (Bosch Ventures) and industry angels and private investors. Fadi Noureddine, founder and Managing Partner of Valquest Partners, has joined the Sonexos Board of Directors.

“Engineers have always had to trade space and weight for silence. Plasmacoustics removes that compromise. This financing carries it from working prototypes into our customers’ products, at scale,” said Mark Donaldson, founder and CEO of Sonexos. 

Sonexos was founded in 2022 by Donaldson, who has built companies in active noise control, including SoundChip, which developed noise-cancelling smart audio codecs for headphones and earbuds from leading consumer electronics brands and was acquired by DSP Group, now part of Synaptics.

Sonexos develops solid-state acoustic technology that solves low-frequency noise where passive materials and speaker-based ANC (active noise cancellation) fall short.

It claims to be developing a new way to address low-frequency noise from fans, compressors and motors. According to the company, this persistent hum carries through walls and windows and is the hardest noise to eliminate. 

It argues that conventional acoustic treatments become increasingly bulky at lower frequencies and can restrict airflow. It further notes that while loudspeaker-based active noise control works well in the confined space of a headphone, it struggles with the complex, three-dimensional sound fields of real-world applications.

The company claims that its patented Plasmacoustic Metalayer uses a software-controlled plasma layer to absorb sound at a surface. The system is thin, lightweight and has no moving parts. 

The Plasmacoustic Metalayer platform enables electronically programmable sound control, allowing compact, lightweight, energy-efficient management of low-frequency noise in domestic appliances, HVAC, and industrial, infrastructure, automotive, and specialised acoustic applications.

The Swiss startup reported that prototype systems have achieved up to 20 dB of low-frequency noise reduction in ventilation systems and 16 dB in domestic appliances under application-specific test conditions.

The company’s Plasmapanel and Plasmadrive technologies are designed to overcome the practical limitations of conventional passive acoustic materials and traditional active noise control systems. 

Sonexos’s Plasmapanel packages the actively controlled plasma metalayer into a sealed, inert-gas-filled module driven by proprietary low-power, high-voltage electronics. The company explains that, depending on the installation, Plasmapanel-enabled systems absorb sound from 30 Hz to 1,500 Hz and, compared with passive silencers with similar low-frequency performance, require less than a fifth of the space and weight. It highlighted that for OEMs, this frees room for more compact products or for features that bulky acoustic treatment would otherwise displace.

Sonexos states that it is developing an industrial ecosystem rather than manufacturing every component in-house. STMicroelectronics is supporting development of low-power, low-cost electronics. A strategic collaboration with Vandewiele Group, through its subsidiary Roj, provides a route toward series manufacturing for European OEM programmes, including electronics production, box-build and cabling.

Sonexos plans to offer turnkey panels with integration support, as well as an enterprise model in which larger OEMs build the technology into their own products and production lines using Sonexos components, such as Plasmadrive, and software.

The company is also planning expansion into AI data-centre cooling, where reduced fan noise could ease community concerns and help sustain cooling capacity under night-time noise limits. It is developing the Plasmapanel Radial Active Silencer to mount around a fan discharge and attenuate low-frequency sound without obstructing the airflow path. 

In July 2026, the company announced a collaboration with Euronext Milan-listed SIT to integrate the technology with fan platforms for data centres, battery energy storage and industrial cooling. SIT is the first member of the Sonexos Certified Fan Partner Programme, and the companies plan to present a first working demonstrator at CES 2027.

“Sonexos is addressing a fundamental engineering constraint with a technology that opens a much larger design space for low-frequency noise control. The combination of differentiated science, a strong intellectual-property position and progress with leading OEMs gives the company a credible path toward industrial production,” said Noureddine.

The fresh capital will fund industrialisation of the core platform; customer integration, reliability testing, qualification, and regulatory compliance; expansion of engineering and applications teams in Switzerland and internationally; and broader international protection of its intellectual property. 

Sonexos holds an exclusive licence from EPFL to grant foundational plasmacoustic patents in its field of use and has filed four additional patent families of its own, with two UK patents granted and applications pending in other major markets.

]]> QuoIntelligence, the Frankfurt-based cybersecurity startup, has received a new investment from Christian Lindner, the former German Federal Finance Minister.

The investment came through his investment vehicle, Christian Lindner Beteiligungsgesellschaft, but the deal’s financial terms were not disclosed. The investment follows the company’s €7.3 million Series A funding round, closed in April 2026 and led by Elevator Ventures, the venture capital arm of Raiffeisen Bank International.

“Europe needs more technology companies that can compete internationally in strategically important markets. QuoIntelligence combines human expertise with AI-driven technology in an area where demand is growing rapidly. I am pleased to support the company as an investor in its next phase of European growth,” said Lindner.

Lindner served as Germany’s Federal Finance Minister from 2021 to 2024 and led the Free Democratic Party (FDP) as its federal Chairman from 2013 to 2025. Before entering politics, he co-founded a successful advertising agency, and through his investment vehicle, he backs early-stage companies as an angel investor.

Founded in 2020 by Marco Riccardi, a veteran Italian cybersecurity expert, QuoIntelligence delivers cyber threat and risk intelligence as a service. Named Europe’s most promising cybersecurity startup 2026 by the European Cyber Security Organisation (ECSO), the company enables organisations to manage cyber risks without having to build a dedicated in-house security team.

The company’s Mercury platform consolidates digital risk protection, cyber threat intelligence, and risk intelligence, spanning geopolitical, physical and compliance exposure, into curated, analyst-reviewed outputs rather than raw data feeds. It also offers KARLA, a conversational AI analyst that makes intelligence accessible across all levels of an organisation.

The company has analysts operating out of Germany, Italy, and Spain, and all customer intelligence data is stored within the EU. QuoIntelligence is ISO27001 certified and serves organisations across finance, transportation, manufacturing, government, and retail, including EU institutions.

“What struck me when I first met Christian Lindner was his entrepreneurial mindset. He immediately focused on the questions that matter to any founder: the market, the business model and the team. That perspective makes him a valuable investor for us. Our ambition is to become the European leader in cyber threat intelligence: a company that European organisations can trust because it understands the risks they face and how they operate,” said Riccardi, founder and CEO, QuoIntelligence.

The Series A funding round and Lindner’s investment come amid a changing regulatory environment that has expanded the market for cybersecurity services. According to QuoIntelligence, NIS2 is expected to bring approximately 29,500 organisations into compliance scope in Germany alone, while the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) has tightened technology risk management standards across the financial sector. Many of these organisations will be required to manage cyber risk without in-house security capabilities.

In 2025, ENISA, the European Union Agency of Cybersecurity, awarded QuoIntelligence a four-year, €1.4 million contract to provide cyber threat intelligence services in an open tender.

When announcing its Series A funding round, QuoIntelligence said it would use the funding for go-to-market expansion, product development, and team growth, with a channel-led strategy through system integrators, resellers, and managed service providers. ]]> Finnish SpaceTech unicorn ICEYE has announced two new partnerships aimed at expanding its satellite intelligence capabilities across defence and environmental monitoring.

The company signed a Letter of Intent alongside Nokia and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore sovereign satellite communications, while also announcing a collaboration with German startup OroraTech to develop an integrated wildfire intelligence solution.

This follows a period of notable growth for the Espoo-based scale-up. In June 2026, ICEYE secured €450 million in primary Series F funding, valuing the company at more than €10 billion, with a further €300 million revolving credit facility secured in May.

This funding activity can be placed alongside adjacent 2026 European SpaceTech funding announcements, including €51 million for Luxembourg and US-based Hydrosat to expand thermal satellite intelligence, €34 million for the UK’s SatVu to scale its thermal observation constellation, and €61 million for Switzerland’s SWISSto12 to develop satellite and communications infrastructure.

In Finland, Helsinki-based Kelluu also raised €15 million to expand its autonomous aerial intelligence capabilities.

Together with funding for France’s UNIVITY (€27 million) and Germany’s AIRMO (€5 million), these 2026 rounds account for approximately €643 million in the general SpaceTech sector, including ICEYE’s primary financing.

Founded in 2014 by Rafal Modrzewski and Pekka Laurila, ICEYE specialises in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite technology, providing Earth observation data and intelligence to governments, defence organisations, insurers and emergency management agencies.

The company originated from research at Aalto University and launched its first SAR satellite in 2018, becoming an early pioneer in miniaturised radar satellites.

The first of the two announcements centres on a Letter of Intent signed by ICEYE, Nokia and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore cooperation on secure satellite communications. Announced during the Finnish Prime Minister’s visit to Ukraine, the initiative aims to strengthen the country’s defence capabilities by developing communications infrastructure that Ukraine can independently own and control.

The agreement builds on an earlier partnership between ICEYE and Nokia, announced on October 1st 2026, to develop secure, high-performance broadband communications systems using low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites. Designed for governments, these systems would support defence, border security, emergency services and disaster response, while giving participating countries control over their satellites, ground infrastructure and terminals.

Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and Co-founder of ICEYE, said: “Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls. We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today.”

ICEYE has supported Ukraine with satellite intelligence since 2022, making the proposed communications collaboration a potential extension of an existing relationship. The latest agreement remains exploratory, with no deployment timetable or financial commitments disclosed.

Alongside its defence-related developments, ICEYE has also partnered with Munich-based OroraTech to expand its wildfire intelligence services. The collaboration will combine OroraTech’s thermal satellite data with ICEYE’s SAR observations, creating a platform intended to help organisations monitor wildfires from their earliest stages through to damage assessment and recovery.

Founded in 2018 by Thomas Grübler, Rupert Amann, Florian Mauracher and Björn Stoffers, OroraTech develops space-based thermal intelligence for wildfire detection and monitoring. The startup has expanded its satellite network and provides information to governments and organisations managing wildfire risks worldwide.

As per our coverage, OroraTech secured a €37 million Series B extension in 2025.

Until now, ICEYE’s wildfire intelligence capabilities have primarily focused on assessing building-level damage during active fires. By incorporating OroraTech’s thermal observations, the company aims to extend its services to include identifying initial hotspots, tracking fire progression and assessing threats to communities and critical infrastructure.

The combination brings together two complementary technologies. OroraTech’s thermal satellites can detect heat anomalies and monitor active fires, while ICEYE’s SAR satellites can capture observations through clouds, smoke and darkness, helping assess damage to buildings and infrastructure even while a wildfire is ongoing.

Dr. Ignacio Zuleta, Chief Technology and Product Officer at OroraTech, commented: “Our thermal satellite intelligence provides that critical visibility from the earliest stages of an event, detecting hotspots and tracking fire activity as it develops. By bringing that intelligence together with ICEYE’s SAR capabilities, we can help decision-makers maintain a more continuous understanding of a wildfire, from first detection through its impact on communities, infrastructure and the surrounding environment.”

The integrated solution targets several sectors, including government emergency management, utilities and insurance. Emergency services could use the intelligence to inform evacuations and coordinate firefighting resources, while energy providers could monitor threats to electricity networks and other infrastructure. Insurers could also use the data to identify exposed properties, assess damage and prioritise claims.

According to ICEYE, the technology could help accelerate disaster response by providing more timely information on wildfire progression and its consequences. The company says its integrated approach could support damage assessments for disaster declarations within 24 hours, compared with processes that can otherwise take weeks.

Taken together, the two announcements are one of many examples of how ICEYE is expanding its satellite capabilities beyond Earth observation imagery into a broader range of intelligence and communications services.

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:49:12 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 Retiring Indian Air Force chief flies final sortie in the same Kiran trainer he first flew in 1984 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/iaf-chief-ap-singh-final-flight-kiran/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 17:38:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54437 India’s Air Chief Marshal AP Singh flew his last sortie in uniform aboard the HJT-16 Kiran trainer at the same air force academy where he first took to the skies in January 1984.

The post Retiring Indian Air Force chief flies final sortie in the same Kiran trainer he first flew in 1984 appeared first on AGN.

]]> For Indian Air Force chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh, the final flight of his military career was not in a frontline fighter jet, but in the modest training aircraft in which he first learnt to fly more than four decades ago.

On 20 October, Singh returned to the Air Force Academy at Dundigal, near Hyderabad in central India, and climbed aboard an HJT-16 Kiran Mk-1 trainer with the man who had taught him to fly, retired Wing Commander VS Kochar.

The 55-minute sortie brought together the same instructor, the same aircraft type and the same training establishment where Singh had taken his first flying lesson on 28 January 1984.

There was even a familiar aircraft awaiting him. The Kiran used for the flight carried the registration U-707.

Singh, who is due to retire as Chief of the Air Staff on 31 October, had wanted his final sortie in uniform to take him back to where his flying career began.

“It was really a dream come true. I started my journey with the same aircraft,” Singh told reporters after landing, according to news agency ANI.

“I think I must be the only chief who’s retiring while the basic aircraft he flew is still serving.”

For a pilot who has spent more than four decades flying military aircraft, the occasion was as much about the instructor sitting beside him as the aircraft itself.

“I’m very grateful to my instructor, VS Kochar sir, who taught me flying in the beginning in this place itself,” Singh said.

“So I just wanted the circle to be complete. And I did my first sortie on 28 January 1984, in this very place with him, and today I did my last sortie in uniform with him in the same aircraft.”

The instructor who started it all

Flying instructors occupy a special place in military aviation. Long before a pilot learns to operate a fighter aircraft, it is an instructor who introduces them to the fundamentals of flight, teaches them to recognise mistakes and develops the judgement needed to handle an aircraft safely.

For Singh, that instructor was Kochar, who was back in the cockpit with his former pupil after 42 years.

The reunion was equally meaningful for the retired officer.

Kochar, now 73, described Singh as his “brightest pupil ever” and the “best chief”, according to comments reported by the Press Trust of India. He said getting another flight with his former student was a dream come true for him as well.

The two men had returned to the academy in very different circumstances from their first flight together. In 1984, Singh was a young trainee beginning his military flying career. This time, he was returning as the head of the Indian Air Force.

Their flight ended with a ceremonial water cannon salute, with jets of water forming an arch over the aircraft as it returned.

The IAF described the occasion as a tribute to the veterans and flying instructors who have shaped generations of its pilots.

Why the Kiran matters

Developed by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), the Kiran is an Indian-designed, single-engine jet trainer that first flew in 1964. It was introduced to prepare pilots for the transition from basic flying instruction to more demanding military aircraft.

The HJT-16 Kiran has been one of the most recognisable aircraft in Indian military flying training.

Its two-seat cockpit allows an instructor and student to fly together, making it particularly suited to teaching jet handling, instrument flying, aerobatics and formation flying.

Unlike modern combat aircraft, the Kiran was not designed around sophisticated sensors, digital displays or advanced weapons. Its principal purpose was to teach pilots how to fly a jet and develop the skills needed for subsequent operational training.

Over the decades, the aircraft became a familiar sight at Indian Air Force training establishments and served as a stepping stone for generations of fighter pilots.

It was also used by the IAF’s Surya Kiran aerobatic team before the team transitioned to the Hawk advanced jet trainer.

The Kiran’s continued service makes Singh’s final sortie particularly unusual. The aircraft type on which he began flying in 1984 was still available for him to fly in October 2026, more than six decades after the design’s first flight.

The IAF has progressively modernised its training fleet with newer aircraft, including the Pilatus PC-7 Mk II basic trainer and the BAE Systems Hawk advanced jet trainer.

However, the Kiran has remained part of the service’s training history, linking successive generations of pilots.

From trainee pilot to air force chief

Singh graduated from the Air Force Academy in 1984, receiving the Sword of Honour, an award recognising outstanding performance during training.

He was commissioned into the fighter stream of the IAF in December that year.

Over the following decades, he qualified as a flying instructor and experimental test pilot, accumulating several thousand hours of flying experience across fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft.

The Rafale F5 is intended to keep France’s principal combat aircraft effective against increasingly sophisticated air defences and new generations of fighters.

Often referred to as the Super Rafale, the proposed upgrade goes considerably further than improvements to radar, communications and weapons.

It is expected to introduce more advanced sensors, electronic warfare capabilities, artificial intelligence and the ability to operate alongside uncrewed aircraft.
