]]> A retired US Air Force (USAF) KC-10A Extender has returned to the skies after spending years in storage at an aircraft boneyard in Arizona. The tanker, formerly designated 86-0034, departed Davis-Monthan Air Force Base on 20 October, beginning a new chapter under private ownership with Omega Air Refuelling.

The aircraft, now registered as N82247, flew to San Antonio International Airport (SAT) in Texas, marking a significant milestone for the company and the retired military tanker fleet.

Its return to flight demonstrates how aircraft once considered destined for museums or spare parts can still have valuable roles in commercial aviation and military support operations.

According to the aviation publication MiGFlug, Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) records identify Omega Air Inc., based in Selma, Texas, as the aircraft’s registered owner. Its registration as a McDonnell Douglas DC-10-30F was issued on 6 October 2026, just over two years after the USAF completed the retirement of its KC-10 fleet.

From military service to the aircraft boneyard

The KC-10 Extender was developed from the civilian DC-10 airliner and adapted to provide aerial refuelling capabilities for the US military. Its combination of three engines, substantial fuel capacity, and versatile refuelling equipment made it an important asset for supporting aircraft on long-distance missions.

The USAF received 60 KC-10s, with deliveries beginning in 1981. One aircraft was destroyed in a ground fire at Barksdale Air Force Base in 1987, leaving 59 to continue serving the fleet.

Retirement began in July 2020, when aircraft 86-0036 became the first KC-10 to leave operational service and fly to the 309th Aerospace Maintenance and Regeneration Group (AMARC) at Davis-Monthan.

The process concluded on 26 September 2024, when the final operational Extender departed Travis Air Force Base in California for storage.

The fleet was retired as the USAF transitioned towards newer tanker capabilities, including the KC-46A Pegasus. However, the departure of the last KC-10 did not necessarily mean the end of the aircraft’s usefulness.

In 2025, ten retired KC-10s were offered for auction through the US General Services Administration. They were sold in non-flyable condition and without their refuelling booms. The aircraft also lacked one wing-mounted engine, meaning buyers faced substantial work before any could return to the air. For N82247, that restoration effort has now resulted in a successful departure from the Arizona storage facility.

Omega Air Refuelling expands its fleet

The aircraft’s new owner, Omega Air Refuelling, is an established contractor providing aerial refuelling services to the US military.

Rather than replacing military tankers in combat operations, companies such as Omega support training, testing and ferry flights, allowing military aircraft to concentrate on operational duties.

Omega already operates former Royal Netherlands Air Force KDC-10 tankers, acquired in 2019, alongside other tanker aircraft.

Adding a former US Air Force KC-10 gives the company another airframe derived from the DC-10 family, an aircraft type with which it has considerable experience.

One particularly important feature of the KC-10 is its original ability to refuel aircraft using both a central boom and a hose-and-drogue system. This combination allows it to support different types of receiver aircraft, including those associated with the US Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps.

Omega has demonstrated the value of its boom-equipped tankers in recent years. In March 2024, one of its KC-10s refuelled a B-52 bomber and an MC-130J aircraft over the Pacific.

n April 2025, another refuelled a C-17 Globemaster III over California. These missions highlight the potential value of the KC-10 platform in contractor-operated refuelling services.

A challenging return to flight

The return of N82247 is particularly noteworthy because the aircraft was not simply waiting in storage in an immediately flyable condition. The ten KC-10s auctioned in 2025 were offered without their refuelling booms and with one wing-mounted engine missing from each aircraft.

Restoring an aircraft to flight under these circumstances requires significant technical work, inspections and coordination to ensure it meets the necessary airworthiness requirements.

The aircraft’s departure from Davis-Monthan therefore represents more than a change of ownership: it demonstrates that at least one retired Extender has successfully completed the work required to fly again.

However, the aircraft’s return should not be confused with a full restoration of its original military capabilities. N82247 departed without its refuelling boom, and Omega has not publicly outlined its complete plans for the aircraft. A boom could potentially be installed again if future contracts require it.

Reports have also indicated that Omega acquired a group of retired KC-10 airframes, although the company’s precise intentions for the remaining aircraft have not been publicly confirmed.

A future beyond military retirement

The KC-10’s story may extend beyond Omega’s commercial operations. In October 2026, reports also indicated that the USAF was seeking industry interest in reactivating up to four stored KC-10s for an unidentified North African partner through the foreign military sales programme.

This possibility highlights the continuing relevance of older tanker aircraft in a world where aerial refuelling remains essential to military aviation.

Reactivating stored aircraft can present substantial challenges, but established designs may still offer useful capabilities when the cost and technical requirements make restoration practical.

For Omega Air Refuelling, N82247 provides an opportunity to expand a fleet built around supporting military aviation. Its existing experience with DC-10-derived tankers gives the company a foundation for operating the aircraft, although its eventual mission profile will depend on its configuration and contractual requirements.

The departure of N82247 from Davis-Monthan Air Force Base is therefore a striking example of an aircraft finding a second life after military retirement.

Once part of a fleet that supported USAF operations around the world, the former 86-0034 has left the Arizona desert under a new registration and a new owner.

]]> A supplier dispute has halted production of Boeing’s 777 Freighter for almost two months, raising concerns over deliveries to major cargo operators including FedEx.

With dozens of aircraft still on order and the next-generation 777-8 Freighter not expected until around 2029, the disruption comes at a critical time for Boeing’s freighter business.

Boeing 777F production halted by supplier dispute

Boeing’s 777 Freighter (777F) production line has been halted for nearly two months following a dispute with Florida-based supplier Vaero, according to a Reuters report published on 23 October.

Despite reaching a settlement with Vaero in late September, Boeing had not resumed production as of 23 October, according to three company workers cited by Reuters. The dispute also affected production of the Boeing 767, including its freighter variant and the KC-46 Pegasus aerial refuelling tanker.

At the centre of the dispute is a fixed trailing-edge rib kit used in the wings of the 777F and 767. Boeing identified Vaero as its sole supplier and alleged in a legal complaint filed in August that the company had stopped delivering the kits.

Without the parts, Boeing could not complete the relevant wing sections, preventing aircraft assembly from progressing at its Everett, Washington, facility.

According to court filings cited by Reuters, Boeing estimated that the disruption was costing it as much as $6.5 million per day. The manufacturer has reportedly begun efforts to bring production of the component in-house, reducing its dependence on a single external supplier.

The effects have already reached the assembly line. Two partially assembled 777Fs were removed because of the shortage. One was identified as destined for FedEx, although the courier did not respond to a request for comment.

Boeing had delivered 21 777Fs during 2026 by the time of the Reuters report. Some further deliveries may still be possible using aircraft whose wings were assembled before the disruption.

Which airlines have Boeing 777F aircraft on order?

The production halt comes as several major cargo operators await new aircraft. Boeing’s order book at the end of September 2026 listed 38 unfilled orders for the current-generation 777F, although some are associated with Russian operators and may not be deliverable under present circumstances.

The outstanding orders include:

  • FedEx Express: Seven aircraft remain on order, making the US cargo giant one of the customers most exposed to potential delays.
  • Saudia: Four 777Fs are listed as outstanding.
  • Emirates: Three aircraft remain on order, following its decision in October 2024 to purchase five additional 777Fs.
  • China Airlines: Two aircraft are listed as outstanding.
  • China Southern Cargo: Two aircraft remain on order.
  • Silk Way West Airlines: Two aircraft are listed in the backlog.
  • Ethiopian Airlines Cargo: Two additional 777Fs were ordered in September 2026.

Another 10 aircraft were attributed to unidentified customers in Boeing’s September order figures, while six remained associated with Russia-linked Volga-Dnepr. Their eventual delivery remains uncertain.

The figures reflect the published order position at the end of September, rather than a confirmed schedule of future deliveries. Boeing has not publicly specified revised delivery dates for customers affected by the production interruption.

Recent deliveries underline continuing demand

Despite the production difficulties, Boeing continued delivering 777Fs during 2026. FedEx and Air China Cargo each received a 777F in September, bringing Boeing’s deliveries of the type to 20 by the end of that month.

Air China Cargo subsequently received another aircraft, its 14th 777F, on 1 October.

Air China Cargo operates its 777Fs alongside Airbus A330 freighters and Boeing 747s, providing capacity across its international cargo network. Ethiopian Airlines, meanwhile, operates 12 777Fs and continues to expand its long-haul freight operations.

Ethiopian Airlines placed a significant order on 30 September, purchasing two additional 777Fs alongside eight next-generation 777-8 Freighters.

The agreement makes Ethiopian the first African airline to order the 777-8F and demonstrates continuing demand for Boeing’s large freighters.

The 777-8 Freighter offers a longer-term solution

Boeing’s production difficulties come amid a transition towards the 777-8 Freighter, the next-generation aircraft intended to succeed the current 777F.

The 777-8F belongs to the 777X family and features a different wing design. Consequently, the supplier dispute affecting the current 777F and 767 does not directly affect the 777X programme.

The new freighter has attracted substantial interest from cargo operators. In July 2026, MSC Air Cargo ordered five 777-8Fs, while Ethiopian Airlines added eight to its order book in September.

Other customers include Qatar Airways Cargo, Cargolux, Korean Air and China Airlines. Cirium’s analysis identifies Qatar Airways as the largest customer, with 34 777-8Fs on order, followed by Cargolux with 10.

However, the new aircraft is not expected to enter service until around 2029, leaving the current-generation 777F important to airlines seeking additional capacity in the intervening years.

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has also granted Boeing an exemption allowing up to 35 additional current-generation 777Fs to receive their first airworthiness certificates between 2028 and 2030.

The decision is intended to help bridge the gap before the 777-8F becomes available, although it does not mean all 35 aircraft have been ordered.

Supply chain resilience remains the immediate challenge

For Boeing, the priority is to restore production and establish a reliable supply of the wing components needed to complete outstanding aircraft.

The dispute demonstrates how a shortage involving a single specialist component can disrupt multiple aircraft programmes, even when demand remains strong and a commercial settlement has been reached.

For FedEx, Saudia, Emirates and other operators awaiting new aircraft, the timing of production recovery will be crucial. The longer the interruption continues, the greater the risk of delivery schedules being pushed back.

With the 777-8F still several years from entering service, Boeing’s ability to resolve the dispute and deliver the remaining 777F backlog will remain a key factor in the availability of new long-haul cargo capacity worldwide.

]]> Airbus is bringing military-grade navigation technology to its A220 passenger jet to help aircraft maintain accurate navigation when GPS signals are jammed, disrupted or deliberately falsified.

The European aircraft manufacturer has selected SkyNaute, an inertial navigation system developed by Safran Electronics & Defense and already used on military platforms. The system is expected to enter service on the A220 around 2030, according to Aviation Week, which reported the timetable following an announcement by Safran executive Benjamin Declety on 21 October.

The decision comes as interference with satellite navigation becomes a growing problem for commercial airlines, particularly on routes passing near military conflicts. Aircraft may suddenly lose reliable GPS information or receive false position data, leaving crews to rely on other navigation systems.

SkyNaute is designed to address that problem by combining satellite navigation with sensors that can independently calculate an aircraft’s movement. When satellite signals become unreliable, the system can continue providing navigation information without depending on GPS.

For Safran, the A220 will be SkyNaute’s first application on a commercial airliner.

Why GPS jamming and GNSS spoofing are growing threats for airlines

Commercial aircraft use satellite navigation to establish their position and support flight management systems. GPS is the best-known service, but it is part of a wider group of satellite navigation networks collectively called Global Navigation Satellite Systems, or GNSS.

These systems have become important to modern airline operations because they provide accurate positioning across long distances, including over oceans and remote regions where ground-based navigation aids may be limited.

The problem arises when satellite signals are deliberately interfered with.

GPS jamming involves transmitting radio signals that overwhelm or block the genuine satellite signals received by an aircraft. The result can be a loss of reliable satellite positioning.

Spoofing is more deceptive. Instead of simply blocking the signal, it involves transmitting false navigation information that can mislead a receiver about the aircraft’s location or time.

The distinction matters. A crew may recognise that GPS has become unavailable, but false position information can be harder to identify, particularly if different aircraft systems begin showing conflicting information.

Interference has become a recurring concern around conflict-affected regions, where military forces use electronic warfare equipment to disrupt satellite-guided weapons, drones and other systems. Civilian aircraft operating in or near these areas can also be affected.

The eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East and areas around the Black Sea and Baltic region have all experienced reports of satellite navigation interference.

Such incidents do not mean an aircraft immediately loses the ability to navigate. Airliners already carry other navigation equipment, and crews have procedures for dealing with unreliable satellite information. However, interference can increase cockpit workload, affect navigation accuracy and complicate operations that depend on satellite positioning.

It is against this background that Airbus is introducing SkyNaute on the A220.

How Safran’s SkyNaute works without GPS

SkyNaute uses a different method of navigation when satellite signals cannot be trusted.

At the centre of the system are three hemispherical resonator gyroscopes, or HRGs, developed by Safran. These sensors measure changes in the aircraft’s orientation using vibrations inside a small, precisely engineered component.

Working with other inertial measurements, the system calculates how the aircraft is moving and estimates its position from a known starting point. It does not need to receive a continuous signal from satellites to do this.

Under normal conditions, SkyNaute combines inertial information with GNSS data to maintain an accurate position. Satellite updates help correct the small errors that gradually accumulate in inertial navigation.

When GNSS information appears unreliable, SkyNaute can identify the discrepancy and rely on its inertial measurements instead.

“We created it for our defense applications, and it brings us the capability to find spoofing situations with a high level of certainty,” Declety told Aviation Week. “Then, the system switches to inertial.”

That does not mean an aircraft can navigate indefinitely without any loss of accuracy. All inertial systems accumulate some error over time. The advantage is that the aircraft retains an independent source of navigation information when satellite signals are lost or manipulated.

Safran says the HRG technology also offers reliability benefits because the gyroscope has no mechanical parts subject to wear.

SkyNaute weighs approximately 3kg, occupies three litres of space and consumes 20 watts of electrical power, according to Safran’s published specifications. Its relatively small size and low power requirements make it easier to integrate into an aircraft without adding substantial weight.

Military technology moves into commercial aviation

SkyNaute was developed for military applications, where aircraft and other platforms must continue operating despite electronic warfare.

Safran says the technology has already been selected for military aircraft, helicopters and drones operated by European armed forces.

These platforms face different operating conditions. Helicopters must cope with strong vibrations, while combat aircraft can experience high manoeuvring loads and deliberate attempts to interfere with their navigation. Uncrewed aircraft may also need to navigate accurately when radio signals are disrupted.

The underlying requirement is the same: a reliable way to establish position and movement without depending entirely on external signals.

The A220 will be the first civil aircraft equipped with SkyNaute. Before introduction, Airbus will need to complete integration testing and the necessary certification work.

Safran also intends to offer the system for retrofit installation, although no airline customers or retrofit timetable have been disclosed.

Safran expands production in France

The move into commercial aviation comes as Safran increases production of the gyroscopes used in SkyNaute.

The technology is developed and manufactured at Montluçon in central France, where the company announced a €120 million ($135 million) investment in June 2026 to expand and modernise its facilities.

Safran plans to increase annual HRG production from 10,000 units to 30,000 by 2032, supporting demand across military and civilian applications.

“Seeing SkyNaute take its place on board the Airbus A220 is a source of immense pride for our teams: for the first time, our inertial navigation system will fly on an airliner. This is a strong signal for French industrial expertise. We sincerely thank Airbus for its trust,” Declety said in Safran’s announcement.

The A220 selection comes as aviation authorities are pressing airlines and manufacturers to prepare for more frequent satellite navigation disruptions.

In March 2026, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) and EUROCONTROL published a joint action plan to improve aviation safety during GNSS interference. EASA followed in July with updated guidance addressing the growing severity and sophistication of jamming and spoofing.

The guidance covers crew training, alternative navigation methods, reporting procedures and better coordination between pilots and air traffic controllers.

]]> Sydney’s new Western Sydney International Airport has welcomed its first international passenger flights, marking the opening of Australia’s first major new airport in more than 50 years.

Air New Zealand flight NZ165 from Auckland landed at Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport on Monday, 26 October, becoming the first international passenger service to arrive at the new airport.

The aircraft later departed for Auckland as flight NZ166, inaugurating a three-times-weekly international connection operating on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.

The milestone follows the airport’s opening to domestic passengers on Sunday, 25 October, when Jetstar operated the first scheduled passenger departure to the Gold Coast.

The A$5.6 billion airport is located at Badgerys Creek, about 60 kilometres west of central Sydney. It was designed to relieve pressure on the city’s existing Kingsford Smith Airport and provide additional capacity for domestic and international aviation.

Sydney’s second airport opens after decades of planning

Western Sydney International has been under development for decades. The Australian government identified Badgerys Creek as the location for Sydney’s second major airport in 1986.

Construction took seven years, with more than 13,000 workers involved in delivering the airport and its associated infrastructure.

The airport’s opening gives Sydney a second major passenger gateway, with facilities designed to accommodate up to 10 million passengers annually in its initial configuration.

The terminal incorporates more than 40 check-in kiosks and 34 automated baggage-drop kiosks, with domestic and international services operating under the same roof.

Its 3.7 km runway can accommodate large long-haul aircraft, allowing the airport to expand its international network as airline demand develops.

The Australian government marked the first passenger departures on 25 October, describing the opening as a milestone for Western Sydney and Australia’s aviation network.

Which airlines will fly from Western Sydney International Airport?

Air New Zealand is the first international airline to operate passenger services from Western Sydney, but several other carriers have confirmed plans to use the airport.

Singapore Airlines is scheduled to begin daily nonstop flights to Singapore Changi Airport on 23 November 2026.

International services are expected to expand further in 2027, with Vietjet planning flights to Ho Chi Minh City in January and Fiji Airways expected to introduce flights to Nadi in March.

Qatar Airways has also announced plans to serve Western Sydney, adding another potential long-haul connection through its Doha hub.

Domestic operations began with Jetstar, which is introducing services to Melbourne, Brisbane and the Gold Coast. The airline’s initial schedule includes up to 14 weekly flights to Melbourne, four to the Gold Coast and three to Brisbane.

Qantas is scheduled to begin operating from the airport on 28 March 2027, using QantasLink Embraer E190 aircraft on services to Melbourne and Brisbane. The airline plans four weekly flights on each route.

Facilities at Western Sydney International Airport

WSI’s terminal was designed for seamless, stress-free and intuitive passenger journeys. The airport will offer several passenger facilities, including retail, food and beverage and lounges.

WSI will open with a selection of cafes and food outlets, with additional venues opening as flight services and passenger numbers grow.

The terminal’s retail offering includes two duty-free shopping areas, various speciality retail outlets, including EyeLove and Tech2Go, and three RELAY stores that offer fresh food, drinks, travel essentials and convenience products.

WSI’s first international lounge—The Rayleigh Lounge—will open in November and be operated by dnata. Eligible Singapore Airlines passengers will enjoy a premium dining and lounge experience, with expansive views of the airfield, fast WiFi, ready access to power outlets to charge their devices, and three private showers.

The terminal was also designed for accessibility and inclusivity, including dedicated sensory spaces for travellers experiencing anxiety or sensory stress, designed by specialist firm Creative Sensory Spaces. 

There are also pet relief rooms for arriving and departing passengers with accredited assistance animals. These rooms are wheelchair accessible and include artificial grassed relief areas, water bowls, waste bags and handwashing facilities.   

Hearing Loop Technology lets travellers with hearing aids or implants hear live announcements and PA messages. People can use the AFILS system by switching their hearing aid or cochlear implants to T switch or telecoil position.  

Dedicated family rooms let parents and carers feed, change and care for infants. Changing places support travellers with complex disability and high support needs beyond the accessible toilets located throughout the airport terminal.  

The airport also has multi-faith, quiet rooms, and ablution rooms available. 

Sydney’s new airport can operate 24 hours a day

One of Western Sydney International’s main operational advantages is its ability to accommodate aircraft movements around the clock.

Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport operates under an overnight curfew restricting most aircraft movements between 11 pm and 6 am.

Western Sydney International does not have the same curfew restrictions, giving airlines greater flexibility to schedule international flights, particularly services connecting Australia with Asia, the Middle East and other long-haul markets.

The airport also has a dedicated 24-hour cargo precinct, which began operations in July 2026.

According to the Australian government’s 26 October announcement, the facility increases Sydney’s air cargo capacity by approximately 33%.

The additional freight capacity is expected to support importers, exporters and logistics operators across Western Sydney.

Western Sydney Airport designed for future growth

The airport forms part of a wider A$18 billion government investment programme in Western Sydney, including road improvements and a new rail connection.

Road access was improved through the M12 motorway. The planned Sydney Metro–Western Sydney Airport line will provide a direct rail connection to the terminal. However, the metro service is not expected to open until late 2027, so passengers will initially have to use road transport, buses and connections to existing rail services.

The airport has been designed for phased expansion beyond its initial annual capacity of 10 million passengers.

For airlines, the new gateway offers additional opportunities to serve Sydney’s western suburbs without relying entirely on Kingsford Smith Airport.

Its location could also make it more convenient for residents and businesses in Western Sydney. Passengers travelling to central Sydney will need to consider the distance and available ground transport.

According to the Australian Government, the “WSI project created over 12,800 jobs,” with around half of those going to local workers.

Construction contributed $500 million to over 360 Western Sydney-based businesses, “including local tradies and construction companies, caterers, and security guards.”

Who was Nancy-Bird Walton and why is Sydney’s new airport named in her honour?

The airport is named after pioneering Australian aviator Nancy-Bird Walton (1915–2009), who became one of the country’s first female commercial pilots.

Born in New South Wales, she learned to fly under Sir Charles Kingsford Smith, whose name is carried by Sydney’s first international airport. She gained her pilot’s licence in 1933 and her commercial licence the following year, becoming the youngest female commercial pilot in the British Commonwealth.

Walton earned the nickname “Angel of the Outback” for flying medical personnel to remote communities in New South Wales during the 1930s. She later trained women during the Second World War and founded the Australian Women Pilots’ Association in 1950.

The Australian government announced the airport’s name in March 2019, recognising her achievements and contribution to Australian aviation.

The airport also celebrates her legacy through artwork and installations in its passenger terminal.

“It is fitting that having recognised Charles Kingsford Smith at Sydney Airport that we now recognise Australia’s greatest female aviation pioneer, Nancy-Bird Walton, in the naming of Western Sydney Airport,” then Prime Minister Scott Morrison said when the airport’s name was announced. 

First international flights mark new chapter for Australian aviation

The Australian government expects Western Sydney International to support tourism, trade and employment as additional airlines begin services.

In the official statement welcoming the first international flights, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said: “Western Sydney is now connected directly to the world, bringing more jobs, more visitors and more opportunities for local businesses.”

The airport’s next major international connection will launch on 23 November, when Singapore Airlines begins its daily Singapore service. 

“It can’t be overstated how big a moment this is for Western Sydney, for its people, for its economy and its industries,” said Catherine King, Minister for Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development and Local Government, during the launch of Jetstar’s domestic services on Sunday. “Today is a real milestone in our country’s travel history, and with tomorrow seeing the first international flight leave the tarmac for Auckland—the sky is the limit.”

]]> Yemen’s Houthi movement says it has targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile. This comes just a day after the Saudi airport partially resumed operations following weeks of disruption.

The latest Houthi missile attack highlights the continuing security challenges facing Saudi Arabia’s aviation sector, with airlines, regulators and airports still assessing the risks posed by an escalating campaign of missile and drone strikes.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed in a statement on X today (26 October) that the group launched a ballistic missile at King Khalid International Airport. He said they also carried out drone attacks against pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s strategic East-West pipeline.

Saree said the attacks achieved their intended objectives, but at the time of publishing the claims had not been independently verified. 

Airlines suspending Riyadh flights: Full list of carriers affected Airlines suspending Riyadh flights: Full list of carriers affected

The announcement came less than 24 hours after Riyadh airport restarted limited operations. The airport had been closed following a series of Houthi attacks earlier this month that caused casualties and widespread disruption to commercial aviation.

Before the reopening, Saree warned international, regional and domestic airlines, along with airport employees and passengers, not to use the facility, describing it as “unsafe” and a military target. He also said the Houthis would continue striking the airport.

Saudi Arabia said its air defences successfully intercepted the latest attack. Saudi military spokesperson Turki Al-Malki said a Houthi ballistic missile bound for Riyadh had been destroyed and confirmed Saudi forces had subsequently carried out strikes against missile launchers and storage facilities inside Yemen.

Airport reopens amid continuing threats

King Khalid International Airport had partially reopened on 25 October, with limited domestic flights and selected international services operated by Saudi carriers.

Under the airport’s phased reopening plan, Terminal 1 has been designated for domestic services, while Terminal 2 is handling international flights operated by national airlines.

Will airlines restart Riyadh flights this weekend? @IndiGo6E has extended Riyadh cancellations until 31 October, while several other carriers are approaching key suspension deadlines. Here’s the latest 👇 https://t.co/JGPelnBUPW

— Aerospace Global News (@Aero_GlobalNews) October 23, 2026

Despite the official reopening, flight activity remains significantly below normal levels. According to airline data experts Cirium, King Khalid International Airport has seen 86% of scheduled flights cancelled since 8 October, with 4,071 of 4,736 scheduled services withdrawn.

International flight cancellations continue

Several international carriers have continued to suspend operations to Riyadh despite the reopening. Last week, IndiGo extended its Saudi Arabia cancellations, while a number of other airlines have postponed the resumption of flights to the Saudi capital.

Operational restrictions also remain in force. Under NOTAM A3650/26, operators require prior approval from Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) for arrivals and departures. A separate notice, A3651/26, prevents airlines from designating Riyadh as a diversion airport.

Advice for passengers

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) recently advised operators to avoid designated areas of Saudi airspace and exercise caution because of missile and drone activity, air defence operations and the risk of misidentification.

The US Federal Aviation Administration has issued separate guidance warning carriers of military activity and potential interference with satellite navigation systems.

According to reports, King Khalid International Airport has been targeted around 20 times since the beginning of October.

Riyadh Air shifts flights to Al Qassim

In light of the attacks, Saudi startup carrier Riyadh Air has confirmed it is temporarily transferring passenger operations from King Khalid International Airport to Prince Naif bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Al Qassim.

In a notice to passengers, Riyadh Air said flights serving Cairo, Dhaka, Jeddah, London Heathrow, Lahore and Islamabad will operate from Al Qassim until further notice.

This means the carrier can continue its international services while security concerns continue around Riyadh.

The move makes Riyadh Air one of the highest-profile airlines to alter operations as a direct result of the attacks and demonstrates the operational challenges facing carriers serving Saudi Arabia.

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {

 }

 function toTitle(s){

 function prettyLabel(kind, slug){

 // Collect facets from the currently-rendered page (used as fallback)
 function collectFacetsFromPage(dock){
 const cards=dock.querySelectorAll('.sie-dock-scroll .program-card');
 const locs=[]; const langs=[]; const lvls=[];
 cards.forEach(c=>{
 const cs=(c.dataset.country||'').trim(); if(cs) locs.push(cs);
 const ls=(c.dataset.languages||'').trim(); if(ls) ls.split(/\s+/).forEach(x=>{ if(x) langs.push(x); });
 const vs=(c.dataset.levels||'').trim(); if(vs) vs.split(/\s+/).forEach(x=>{ if(x) lvls.push(x); });
 });
 const freq=(a)=>{ const m=new Map(); a.forEach(v=>m.set(v,(m.get(v)||0)+1)); return [...m.entries()].sort((A,B)=>B[1]-A[1]).map(x=>x[0]); };
 return { locations:freq(locs), levels:freq(lvls), languages:freq(langs) };
 }

 function cardMatchesFilters(card){

 }
 if (state.levels.size){
 const lvls=(card.dataset.levels||'').split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);

 }
 if (state.languages.size){
 const langs=(card.dataset.languages||'').split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
 if(!langs.length || !langs.some(l=>state.languages.has(l))) return false;

 // Render pagination from server-provided total
 function renderPagination(dock){
 const wrapper = dock.querySelector('#program-results-wrapper');
 const totalAll = Number(wrapper?.dataset.total || 0);
 const perPage = parseInt(wrapper?.dataset.perPage || state.pageSize, 10);
 const pages = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(totalAll / perPage));
 if(state.currentPage > pages) state.currentPage = 1;
 const pager = dock.querySelector('.sie-pager'); if(!pager) return;
 pager.innerHTML = '';
 const btn = (label, opts={})=>{
 const b=document.createElement('button'); b.type='button'; b.className='sie-page-btn'; b.textContent=label;
 if(opts.disabled) b.setAttribute('disabled','disabled');
 if(opts.page) b.setAttribute('data-page',opts.page);
 if(opts.active) b.classList.add('active');
 pager.appendChild(b);
 };
 btn('‹ Prev',{disabled:state.currentPage<=1, page:state.currentPage-1});
 const win=5; let start=Math.max(1,state.currentPage-2), end=Math.min(pages,start+win-1);
 if(end-start<win-1){ start=Math.max(1,end-win+1); }
 for(let p=start;p<=end;p++){ btn(String(p),{page:p,active:p===state.currentPage}); }
 btn('Next ›',{disabled:state.currentPage>=pages, page:state.currentPage+1});
 }

 function sieOvvEsc(s){

 }
 function proxyPopoverChip(dock, which, val){

 // Union-merge: options that exist WITHOUT filters but are zeroed by the
 // current combination render with (0), dimmed — options never disappear
 // (same rule as the Leonardo overview).
 function sieOvvMergeBase(cur, base){
 function mergeArr(curA, baseA, keyFn){
 const have = new Set((curA||[]).map(keyFn));
 const extra = (baseA||[]).filter(x=>!have.has(keyFn(x))).map(x=>Object.assign({}, x, {count:0}));
 return (curA||[]).concat(extra);
 }
 return Object.assign({}, cur, {
 fields:    mergeArr(cur.fields,    base.fields,    x=>x.key),
 levels:    mergeArr(cur.levels,    base.levels,    x=>x.slug),
 fees:      mergeArr(cur.fees,      base.fees,      x=>x.key),
 locations: mergeArr(cur.locations, base.locations, x=>x.slug)
 });
 }

 });

 ov.fields.slice(0,8).forEach(f=>{

 const locActive = s => state.locations.has(s) || initLocs.has(s);

 + '</span>';

<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>

                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support measures are provided to staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants. For example:  allocation of additional resources, training on intercultural competences and other relevant aspects of the mob</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should allocate additional resources to support staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants, such as allowing staff adequate time to carry out work with outgoing and incoming participants and providing administrative back-up (e.g. with financial management). Trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, management of mobility projects’, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for Erasmus+ mobility</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>

                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on shared quality requirements, student and staff selection for mobility and clear timelines at all stages of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>A key role of Inter-Institutional Agreements is to set out agreed, shared quality criteria and clear timelines for all stages of the mobility.<br>Shared quality criteria may include, but are not limited to: selection criteria for the nomination of students and staff, recommended language skills, grading systems, measures for preparing, receiving and integrating Erasmus+ participants. These might be expanded with geographic and subject-specific criteria.<br>In terms of the timelines set out for the mobility activities, particular attention should be paid to:</p><ul><li>The nomination of mobile students by the sending HEI,</li><li>The acceptance of nominees, and</li><li>The issuing of the Transcript of Records after the study period abroad by the receiving HEI. This is normally issued within five weeks after the end date of the mobility period.</li></ul>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">There are specific provisions e.g. in the general policies, rules and regulations of the institution</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. The institution must clearly demonstrate through its policies, rules and regulations that equal access and opportunities to mobile participants from all backgrounds. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The principle - that extra fees are not being charged to incoming mobile students - is implemented</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The receiving institution must <strong>not </strong>charge any type of fees to incoming mobility students for the tuition, registration or examination of these students or for their access to laboratory, library and other facilities offered to local students.<br>In certain cases, however, mobile students may be required to pay small fees for insurance, student unions, use of miscellaneous materials (e.g. photocopies, laboratory products) on the same basis as these are charged to local students. Students should be made aware of these extra costs before the start of mobility. Fees may only be charged in the case of full degree mobility or for students registered in joint degree programmes.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All students and staff (incoming and outgoing) are treated equally in all academic and service matters</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In accordance with equal access and opportunities, all students and staff should be treated equally in all academic and service matters. Clear appeal procedures should be in place to ensure equal treatment. There should be individuals - such as mentors and counsellors - available to offer support.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides incoming mobile participants with access to the same services and facilities available to local students and staff</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital to ensure that incoming mobility participants have full access to the same services and facilities as local students and staff. For example, mobility participants with special needs can benefit from the support services that the receiving institution offers to its local students and staff.</p>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Before the mobility, your institution has established formal procedures for recognising student mobility (good practices linked to e.g. the use of Learning Agreements)</div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> At the end of the mobility, your institution has formal procedures for recognising student mobility (good practices linked to recognition at the end of the mobility, e.g. in the use of Transcripts of Records and Grade Distribution Tables)</div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records are issued in a timely manner (normally 5 weeks) to both incoming and outgoing students</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is highly important in the recognition framework to provide Transcripts of Records in a timely manner, immediately following the mobility period. After the mobility, the receiving institution should send a Transcript of Records to the student and to the sending institution within a period stipulated in the Inter-Institutional Agreement (normally within five weeks after publication/proclamation of the student’s results at the receiving institution). It can be provided electronically or through any other means accessible to the student and the sending institution. The Transcript of Records from the receiving institution should refer to the educational components agreed upon in the Learning Agreement. Grade distribution information should be included as well, either as a web link or an annex.</p><p>Following the receipt of the Transcript of Records from the receiving institution, the sending institution should automatically transfer and recognise the student’s academic outcomes successfully completed at the receiving institution, as agreed in the Learning Agreement, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. The Sending Institution will provide a Transcript of Records to the student or record the results in a database or any other means accessible to the student, normally within five weeks after having received the transcript of the receiving institution. The EU official template for the Learning Agreement for studies (including the Transcript of Records) is available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records of incoming students include, where applicable, a Grade Distribution Table for the programme of study, according to the ECTS Users’ Guide</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Where applicable, the Sending Institution should translate the grades received by the student abroad. To enable the Sending Institution to do so, it is highly important for the receiving institution to provide a clear explanation of the institutional grading system and grade distribution in the department or study programme together with the Transcript of Records. Such information can be provided either through a web link or as an annex to the Transcripts of Records. Where applicable, use should be made of a Grade Distribution Table for the programme of study, according to the ECTS Users’ Guide (<a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm</a>).</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All credits gained by students during a period of study abroad that were specified in the final version of the Learning Agreement are automatically transferred by your institution and count towards the students' final degree, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The sending institution should ensure that all the credits earned by the mobile student during the mobility period are recognised and counted towards the final degree, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. The period of study abroad must be clear in the student's records and documents issued to the student (Diploma Supplement or equivalent). This is a golden rule of recognition of credit mobility within the framework of inter-institutional agreements. All the credits towards the student's degree that are earned during the mobility period and which were originally agreed on in the Learning Agreement (or a revised version to it) should be recognised by the sending HEI without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. Learning Agreements are binding for all the parties and require that, on successful completion of the mobility period, the sending HEI recognises credits earned by the student and documents these credits in the student records, so they can be identified in a transparent way.</p><p>Upon receipt of the Transcript of Records or Training Certificates, the sending HEI should:<br>a) certify the mobile student has fulfilled all requirements stipulated in the Learning Agreement;<br>b) ensure recognition of the mobility period abroad within the time-scale and according to the conditions stipulated in the institutional recognition framework.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">In addition to recognising formal learning, the institution recognises any non-formal or informal learning acquired during the mobility according to the ECTS Users’ Guide, e.g. by awarding ECTS credits for volunteering</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>During a period of mobility, students often take advantage of other opportunities outside of their required courses. These may include specific activities which can be considered non-formal or informal learning where they have acquired new skills. This could include additional language and cultural courses, extra-curricular activities, setting up a business and volunteer work undertaken by the student in that period or upon return at the receiving institution.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/standing-out-from-the-crowd-supporting-students-through-full-recognition-and-documenting-of-mobility-outcomes" target="_blank">"Standing out from the crowd" - supporting students through full recognition and documenting of mobility outcomes</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/a-common-approach-to-ects-grade-conversion-ensuring-a-fair-assessment-of-student-performance-after-study-abroad" target="_blank">A common approach to ECTS grade conversion, ensuring a fair assessment of student performance after study abroad</a></div>
                                             </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close-text"><i class="fa fa-times fa-2x"></i><span>Close</span></div>
                </div>
            </div>
